Figure 2 shows our scenario analysis for plausible BoE paths. Both trades perform with similar P&L in our base case. records.text: While the breakeven rate provides a useful benchmark for the number of jobs needed to keep the unemployment rate stable, the actual number in a given month—or even over a multi-month period—can be quite different from the estimates derived from either approach discussed above. records.text: you put in. Refining is therefore fundamentally a zero-sum game. Producing more of one fuel usually means producing less of another. In high-complexity refiners (like those common in the US) volumetric yields are often heavily skewed toward gasoline. Because the global passenger car fleet is so large, modern refiners are heavily optimized toward gasoline production. To do so, they rely on “crackers” that break heavier hydrocarbon molecules into lighter, gasoline-range products, boosting gasoline output well beyond what a barrel of crude would naturally yield. For example, without fluid catalytic crackers (FCCs), the natural gasoline yield from crude might be around 20%; with them, gasoline yields in highly complex refineries can rise to 45% or more (Figure 1). Jet fuel occupies the middle portion of the barrel—sitting between gasoline and diesel in the distillation column—and, depending on refinery configuration, typically accounts for roughly 8-15% of refinery output (Figure 2). Diesel molecules are larger and heavier than gasoline molecules, which is why diesel contains more energy per gallon and remains the preferred fuel for heavy-duty trucking, shipping and many industrial applications. Along with other middle distillates, diesel typically makes up roughly 25-35% of refinery yields. Ad-hoc model: Korea, Japan, India and Australia Korea, Japan, India and Australia sit between quasi-regulated and liberalized regimes. These markets are broadly market-based in normal times, but governments may lean on refiners, state-linked firms, or tax policy to smooth pump prices during shocks. Interventions tend to be temporary and need-based rather than structural, with support delivered through tax cuts, margin compression, and selective relief measures. In Korea, the Industry Ministry imposed in Mar temporary maximum supply prices on gasoline, diesel, and kerosene, an emergency tool unused since the Asian Financial Crisis (Exhibit 8). This marks the strongest energy‑market intervention in nearly 30 years (See note, Korea Watch: First fuel price cap introduced in 30 years marks active policy measures on the way). Meanwhile, Japan reinstated gasoline subsidies on 19 March. Under the scheme, the government fully absorbs, via subsidies, the portion of the nationwide average retail gasoline price that exceeds ¥170/liter (see Exhibit 9 and our note, Japan Viewpoint: Cost of energy subsidies: rising risk of a supplementary budget ahead of summer). The influence of domestic politics, primarily via the long-end, is more subtle, but it is showing and may increase in the aftermath of the local elections. This creates bear-steepening risk in the coming weeks and makes it more likely that 10yr gilts can sustain a move above 5%, although that primarily depends on the conflict. Geopolitics via the front-end is the primary driver. It is fair to the say that the bulk of the volatility in gilt yields and curve is being driven by headlines concerning the potential reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. At the time of print, oil prices are down sharply on the week with hopes of progress towards a deal. How this develops will be key to whether the 5% level in 10yr yields – which gilts have closed above twice in the last couple of weeks – is a peak. We opted to fade BoE pricing relative (to the ECB) rather than outright. If the Strait does reopen, there is plenty of BoE hike premium left to take out (with about 50bp of hikes priced to December vs 80bp just before last week’s BoE meeting). Likewise, by the end of the third year following the shock, late tightening leads to a substantially larger nominal rate of 1.4pp (relative to cases where central banks follow a standard Taylor rule, Figure 1). Higher inflation expectations likely to lead to a higher terminal rate All in all, we think that BanRep’s surprise hold could lead to an increase in inflation expectations of at least 0.3pp initially, which is likely to grow due to: ▪ Greater transmission of upside inflation surprises (which are more likely in the current context); and ▪ The effects of a delayed tightening, since the last rate hike was in March and the next could be at the end of June, with a risk that it occurs only in September with a change in government. An increase in inflation expectations of 0.3–1.0pp could lead to a higher terminal rate of 0.5–1.5pp, we estimate. Sources: Bloomberg Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: AUDZAR longs have built with the move higher in spot AUDZAR has rallied by over 4% since the start of the Middle East conflict and for good reason as Australia is a net energy exporter and South Africa a net energy importer. Notably the AUDZAR-oil correlation is now close to an all-time high as a result (Figure 2). Additionally, Reserve Bank of Australia tightening as well as possible superannuation fund FX hedging may have helped the cross to perform. We hold a structurally bullish view on the AUD and the medium-term bullish AUD factors have not changed much, in our view. On a sequential basis, consumer prices rose 0.1% mom (NSA), driven by transportation prices. According to the latest Manufacturing PMI survey, cost pressures have further intensified in April - the input price index rose by the largest extent since 2022. Philippines CPI inflation surprised sharply to the upside in April, rising 7.2% yoy n versus Bloomberg consensus expectations of 5.5%. Price pressures were broad-based: beyond transport, consumer prices also increased across food and housing utilities, pointing to signs of secondary pass-through from higher energy prices. Indonesia’s real GDP accelerated to 5.6% yoy in Q1 2026, up from 5.4% yoy in Q4 n 2025, surprising to the upside. Contemporary measurement began in 1947. Whether we look at employee compensation, add proprietor’s income, or make the denominator national income, domestic income, or output, 2026Q1 looks set to see income from labor be the lowest on record. Labor's share is the fraction of economic output, in current dollars, that accrues to workers in the form of compensation. Because of the theoretical equivalence between concepts such as Gross Domestic Income and Gross Domestic Output, the term can be redefined as a share of output, such as the output of the nonfarm business sector published by the BLS this week (54.1%) and shown below. Or we can compute employee compensation as a share of national or domestic income, also shown below. The BLS measure includes the self-employed, and business sector components of the government such as the post office. The red line we show below is all economy, including government and proprietors' income. records.text: Are Rising Energy Prices Detrimental to the Japanese Economy? For Japan, an energy-importing country, higher energy prices weigh on national income via deterioration in terms of trade, acting to depress economic growth (Exhibit 1). As income and expenditure are closely related, this effect tends to manifest relatively early. However, higher energy prices can be positive for the national economy as a whole over a slightly longer-term horizon, potentially boosting productivity and competitiveness by encouraging the development of energy-saving technologies and a transition to an energy-efficient economy. In this context, the Cabinet Office (2010) pointed out that the two oil shocks from the mid-1970s to the early 1980s led to a shift in Japan’s economic structure, with energy-intensive industries replaced by energy-efficient industries as key drivers and contributing to the subsequent strong performance of the Japanese economy.1 In this report, we provide an overview of how Japan’s economy has evolved from the perspective of energy consumption and examine the potential for energy efficiency to have a positive impact on the Japanese economy over a slightly longer-term horizon. Japan has a track record of improving its energy efficiency during periods of rising crude oil prices. In particular since 2000, a period in which crude oil prices have remained elevated, its energy efficiency has improved continuously. By making semiannual reporting optional, we think the SEC is testing whether the market can determine appropriate disclosure frequency. The EU, UK, Hong Kong, and Japan already provide for semiannual reporting. 2. How is the new semiannual report different from the current quarterly report? The new Form 10-S generally would require the same auditor-reviewed financial statements and narrative disclosure required by Form 10-Q but for a six-month period rather than a quarter. The Form 10-S filing deadline (40 or 45 days depending on filer status) would match the current Form 10-Q deadline. 3. When would companies opt in and what would be their choices? Companies would have to elect at the beginning of their fiscal year (when they file their Form 10-K for the prior fiscal year) whether they would be semiannual or quarterly filers and could not switch reporting frequency midyear. Based on a combination of considerations, the SEC anticipates that companies would choose one of three reporting categories: quarterly reporter, semiannual reporter, or hybrid reporter (mandatory semiannual reporting with voluntary quarterly disclosures through earnings releases, earnings guidance, or conference calls). 4. records.text: US Rates Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 19 Financing estimates – TGA to increase in Q3 On Monday, Treasury released their financing estimates for Q2 and Q3 2026. For Q2 2026, Treasury stated that they expect to borrow $189bn in private net- marketable debt. For Q3, Treasury expects $671bn in financing needs. For now, we expect slightly higher Q3 needs due to uncertainty around tariff refunds and potential for additional defense spending. On TGA, as we had previously warned (US Rates Weekly - May refunding preview – Will auction sizes ever be increased?), Treasury guided to an end of Q3 TGA balance of $950bn, which is higher than our previous estimate of $900bn. We think there is a strong chance that $950bn is the new steady state for TGA since in recent years Treasury has not reduced its TGA target once it is increased (the exception we found was in Q4-24 due to the debt ceiling). Near term, the TGA balance is likely to move lower into mid-May before increasing towards June-end. And Treasury anticipates that the TGA balance could reach $1tn +/- $50bn in late July and mentioned that it is driven by the “large outflows expected to occur at that time.” A larger TGA balance will, in our view, reduce incentives for the Fed to slow down significantly or stop reserve management purchases in the near term. (See Chart 1) The main consideration for issuers calling outstanding deals is the impact on the underlying loan pool (if called). The two common exit routes are re-securitization (relever) or whole loan sale. The relative profitability of each route drives the final call decision. Beyond excess spread, in our view, GWAC of the underlying loan pool is emerging as a key driver . A high GWAC level makes deal redemption more likely , whereas a low GWAC pool usually depresses the motivation of both exit options. Looking at the outstanding NQM transactions from 2022, 18 deals have now crossed their 4yr coupon step-up date and excess spread has been squeezed by ~ 70bp on average. The excess spread of 4 deals turned to negative post step up and start ed to cumulate coupon cap shortfalls . The reason why these deals are still outstanding, in our view, was mainly due to insufficient GWAC of the loan pool with a mid-4% av erage and issuers found it difficult to figure out a viable exit route, especially for the whole loan sale option. Since GSEs do not buy NQM loans and issuers/lenders are reluctant to retain loans on their balance sheet , the loan sale would need to be at a discount given the lower GWAC in turn erodes issuers’ benefits. In fact, a closer look at earnings season results to date shows that companies with the most debt are also growing earnings much faster than the average company, e.g. many of them could delever organically given their earnings trajectory but are instead in some cases choosing to add debt to maintain their strong earnings growth prospects (the hyperscalers being a key example of this construct). For this analysis, we bucketed the ~380 S&P500 companies that have reported so far by their total debt footprint (not IG bond index debt, in order to include the likes of commercial paper issuance etc) and calculated simple average earnings growth y/y for each cohort. The second biggest acceleration in S&P 500 earnings growth this quarter has come from the cohort with the most debt: The 42 companies with $50bn+ in total debt saw earnings growth surge to 28.1% y/y from just 7.1% last quarter, a +21 point improvement that is more than double the overall acceleration of +9.7 points (24% versus 14%). Media reports (see here, here, here) suggest possible political volatility following the local elections, with investor focus on the path ahead for fiscal policy. We have outlined our latest thoughts here, and the £10 billion hit to headroom from the effects of the closure of Hormuz remains our base case. The government is likely, we think, to provide targeted support to households in the autumn should utility bills remain elevated, with low chance of the September fuel duty hike going ahead, we think. £5 billion seems to us the very top end of the plausible one-off package. Looking ahead, we continue to flag two key areas of focus for us: given day-to-day spending growth in real terms is due to flatline from 2027, we see the Spending Review next year as the key upcoming fiscal juncture. And we take the explicit endorsement of the March path (and of the March path’s peak) as a signal that upside surprises in the macro data will be needed to hike again in the near term. While the weak starting point in inflation keeps the Riksbank relatively comfortable right now, the increase in corporate cost pressures and pricing plans are more concerning for the medium-term outlook. In other words, the returns would not only be small but only exist in certain repo environments, such as when reserves conditions tighten (for instance as the TGA rises). But this presents an opportunity for Treasury to deploy that excess cash into repo whenever repo rates move over IORB, counteracting the effects of a rising TGA. That would make the Treasury a notable marginal cash investor in potentially large size, likely helping suppress funding market pressures. Smooth funding markets likely benefit Treasury in other ways, such as supporting swap spreads, and in turn reducing the cost of issuance further out the curve. Structural reforms to the welfare state system and healthcare insurance regimes should come on top, and might not impact the federal budget per se, but household disposable income may be hit (EUR 16bn in savings are planned for next year). For instance, in the QRA Treasury noted the policy indicates that it needs to have $1tn on hand at the end of July to meet its outflow needs, and when the TGA reaches that level their would be no excess to invest. As a result, simply investing “excess" cash above the minimum requirement would do little to support a structurally smaller Fed balance sheet. TBAC discussed an alternative framework in which Treasury would hold only three days of projected outflows in the TGA, with days four and five placed into the repo market. Outflows associated with days four and five can be sizable as well, particularly around coupon settlements, suggesting that this approach would also need to be capped to avoid large and abrupt swings in the amount the Treasury is investing. But importantly, designing the program this way would would give Treasury an available cash balance to deploy even when the required minimum is very high, meaning that Treasury can move into repo as the balance peaks and the drain on reserves is extreme. That would give it meaningful capacity to counteract the effects of a rising TGA on repo markets directly. In short, if the objective is to earn a return on the excess cash, that direct return is likely marginal and dependent on the repo environment. records.text: The Breakeven Rate Debate: How Many Jobs Do We Need to Create? Labor supply growth declined sharply as immigration fell from its 2023 peak, and we expect it to slow further in 2026. In our recent work, we estimated that net immigration declined from a peak of 2.4mn in 2023 to 0.4mn annualized in recent months and should slow further to 0.2mn in 2026. Recently released Census population projections show that native-born population growth is also set to decline in 2026. Together, these estimates imply a meaningful slowdown in growth of the civilian noninstitutional population from 2mn in 2025 (0.8%) to 1.2mn in 2026 (0.4%). What does this mean for the pace of job growth needed to keep the unemployment rate stable? In our baseline analysis, we assume that labor force participation rates of native-born workers follow the CBO’s projected potential path and those of recent immigrants follow our estimated path. This approach suggests that the breakeven rate has slowed to 65k in recent months and should fall further to 50k by year-end (Exhibit 2). records.text: Dividend payments in Asia are often concentrated at certain points in the year, and can be meaningful in size. The annual dividends paid by companies on major local equity indices have consistently represented between 1–8% of local GDP since 2015 (Figure 2), depending on the market in question. Over the past five years there have been several instances where dividend payments in South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore or Thailand have reached >1% GDP in a single month (Figure 3). In recent years, annual dividend payments in these regions, as a percentage of GDP, have also trended higher. Estimates for 2026 dividend payments collected by Bloomberg suggest these patterns are likely to remain, and may even be stronger than in recent years, with annual payments predicted to exceed the five-year average in most economies. The proportion of dividends due to be paid to foreign investors is particularly high in economies like South Korea, Taiwan, Indonesia and India. records.text: 4 US Economic Viewpoint | 07 May 2026 1. K-shaped balance sheets At the core of the K-shaped spending outcome is a growing divergence in household balance sheets. Asset exposure, leverage, and sensitivity to interest rates differ sharply across the income and age distribution, shaping how households have absorbed post- pandemic shocks, market performance, higher for longer rates, tighter financial conditions. These asymmetries show up most clearly in two dimensions: net worth accumulation and credit stress, which together anchor the balance-sheet “K” shaping consumer behavior. Net worth Household wealth has been surging. The gains since the start of the pandemic have been led by equities (Exhibit 5). Equities account for more than half the $42tn increase in total assets since 4Q 2022. But the improvement has been highly uneven across the income distribution. Measures of household assets relative to liabilities show that gains have been far larger for households at the top of the income distribution than for those at the bottom (Exhibit 6), with equities accounting for most of the divergence (Exhibit 7). records.text: 7 May 2026 Europe Blog Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Energy shock, waning economic momentum and the fiscal question The Iran shock is undoubtedly inflicting economic damage. Recent hard and soft data indicate that the Euro Area is drifting towards an unwelcome state of stagnation, if not worse. Q1 GDP growth softened to just 0.1% q/q, falling below consensus expectations and decelerating from the 0.2% q/q recorded at the end of last year. Initial data for Q2 suggest a further loss of economic momentum. The Composite PMI for activity dropped below the 50-point expansion-contraction threshold in April, while consumer confidence is in near free-fall. While Q1 GDP growth may have been dragged lower by Irish volatility, the broad-based decline in soft data suggests this loss of momentum extends beyond mere statistical fluctuations. Conversely, inflationary pressures are mounting. Euro Area inflation rose to 3% yoy in April, driven admittedly by an energy surge. Firms' selling price expectations are on the rise (for more see our recent blog " Passthrough Playbook: Tracking the stages of energy transmission ), as are household short- and long-term inflation expectations, according to our in-house (dbDatainsights) survey. Against this backdrop, several Euro Area governments have implemented fiscal measures to counter the shock (for more go here). The new draft plan anticipates net funding needs of EUR 196.5bn for 2027 (4.3% of GDP). Only around half of that is “easing” via increased defence spending in the core budget. The rest is a level shift from cyclical weakness. records.text: ab 8 May 2026 Global Research US Economic Data NFP likely to fuel the hawkish tone Nonfarm payroll employment posts solid gain Nonfarm payroll employment expanded 115K in April, a little ahead of our expectations (100K) and above consensus (65K). We attributed some of the April NFP strength to the pandemic's undue influence on seasonal adjustment, which after looking through the details we still think is the case. The increase also got a boost relative to our expectations from the now-famous residual net birth death adjustment. Preceding months gains were revised down -16K. Our assessment of the trend in nonfarm payroll employment of say ~50K jobs per month in the published data remains. That's not much different than the 3, 6, 8 month moving averages. The 4-month moving average is getting some help from the base effects (January strength undoing December weakness), and we expect that April likely revises lower in the next two reports, which has been the tendency in recent years. Note that assessment of the trend in the published data does not account for the monthly survey overstatement. For the FOMC, another decent month of job gains, nothing bad happening, and decent internals, reinforces the resilience theme. That in turn should fuel the hawkish narrative and embolden the hawks among the FOMC participants to make their case that the risks that need to be addressed are the upside risks to inflation rather than worry about downside risks to the labor market. Strategic US acquirors have announced nearly $700 billion in M&A YTD, 140% higher than at the same point in 2025. Sponsor M&A growth has been weaker, totaling $190 billion (-37% year/year). We forecast completed cash M&A for the S&P 500 will grow by +80% in 2026 and +15% in 2027. From a macro perspective, M&A activity will be supported by resilient CEO confidence, solid US economic growth, and relatively easy financial conditions. M&A will also benefit from the combination of a friendly regulatory backdrop and a desire for AI-related business transformation. Our forecast for completed M&A is sensitive to the closing timelines of a few large deals that have already been announced. The cash component of M&A activity has remained close to recent averages despite high equity valuations. Companies historically have shifted towards share-based compensation when valuations are elevated. However, cash has represented nearly 70% of announced M&A deal value YTD. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 08 May 2026 10:08:25 ET │ 11 pages US Economics Softer details of strong April jobs data CITI'S TAKE Payroll employment rose by 115k jobs in April, much stronger than the modest decline we were expecting and breaking the recent pattern of job growth oscillating between positive and negative each month. But payroll data still seems very volatile to us, and we would expect weaker readings into the summer months, as has been the trend the last few years. The unemployment rate remains the most important detail of monthly jobs reports and rose on an unrounded basis to 4.34% from 4.26% despite another decline in labor force participation. We also expect this trend to shift into the summer hiring months when new graduates and students enter the labor force. We continue to expect familiar patterns of the unemployment rate breaking above its recent range in late summer to have Fed officials cutting rates again in September. records.text: Asia Viewpoint | 07 May 2026 7 Inflation stability is a key concern, but not the only one Since the outbreak of the Middle East tensions, policymakers’ primary focus have shifted to price stability by managing the initial supply shock, and containing any potential second-round effects. In our view, an economy with 1) a more liberalized fuel market, 2) higher energy import dependence, and 3) less fiscal buffer to provide cost-of-living relief measures tend to have stronger tightening bias to anchor inflation expectation. The Philippines is a clear example of how oil‑driven inflation could alter policy direction. CPI inflation accelerated sharply to 7.2% yoy in Apr, putting pressure on the PHP and reinforcing the need for further policy tightening to anchor price and FX stability. If the BSP remains confident that inflation has not become unanchored and FX pressures are not driven by excessive speculation, it may wait until the June meeting before raising rates. As a result, we expect 25bp hike in June and Aug respectively to bring policy rate to 5.00%. Still expect divergent policy path across Asia That said, despite the inflationary pressure across the region, we still expect divergent paths ahead (Exhibit 10, also see note, Asia Viewpoint: Policy responses vary against rising stagflationary risks). Meanwhile on the liabilities side, credit cards and auto loan delinquencies are elevated and still rising. This disproportionately hurts younger, lower- income households. K-shaped housing market Housing costs have reinforced this divergence. The homeownership rate for older, higher-income households has increased by roughly 10pp since the 1980s, while it has remained largely flat among younger households. And, rental inflation has risen far more sharply over the last few years than mortgage payments, since most homeowners are still locked into low fixed-rate pre-pandemic mortgages. Hence, housing-related costs have been borne disproportionately by renters who tend to have lower-income. K-shaped labor market Higher-income wage growth has been outpacing lower-income for over a year. This reflects i) low labor market turnover hurting younger, lower-income workers who switch/ look for jobs more often, and ii) weaker junior hiring due to payback for post-pandemic over-hiring and AI adoption in some sectors. Hence, the unemployment rate rose faster among younger workers, peaking at nearly a 10-year high of 9.2% in 2H25. This exacerbated K-shaped spending dynamics because these workers rely more on labor income to fuel spending. records.text: you put in. Refining is therefore fundamentally a zero-sum game. Producing more of one fuel usually means producing less of another. In high-complexity refiners (like those common in the US) volumetric yields are often heavily skewed toward gasoline. Because the global passenger car fleet is so large, modern refiners are heavily optimized toward gasoline production. To do so, they rely on “crackers” that break heavier hydrocarbon molecules into lighter, gasoline-range products, boosting gasoline output well beyond what a barrel of crude would naturally yield. For example, without fluid catalytic crackers (FCCs), the natural gasoline yield from crude might be around 20%; with them, gasoline yields in highly complex refineries can rise to 45% or more (Figure 1). Jet fuel occupies the middle portion of the barrel—sitting between gasoline and diesel in the distillation column—and, depending on refinery configuration, typically accounts for roughly 8-15% of refinery output (Figure 2). Diesel molecules are larger and heavier than gasoline molecules, which is why diesel contains more energy per gallon and remains the preferred fuel for heavy-duty trucking, shipping and many industrial applications. Along with other middle distillates, diesel typically makes up roughly 25-35% of refinery yields. Energy Sigma Deal or no deal Oil markets have been oscillating between hopes of a potential deal to end the war and the threat of renewed aggression. Meanwhile, ME oil exports remain heavily restricted and inventories continue to draw at a fast pace. We maintain our $100/b Brent forecast for 2026 with risks skewed higher. • Iran's response to the US proposal to end the war is still pending, and despite a few incidents of late, the fragile ceasefire continues to hold. Even in the most optimistic scenario, we think, oil prices are probably too low, as demand remains largely resilient and inventories continue to draw fast. • SPR, spare capacity and even the potential US supply response are all skewed toward addressing the crude supply issue, but refined product supply is a bigger constraint, especially for middle distillates. We therefore recommend going long the December 2026 ICE Gasoil minus Brent crack spread at $33.4/b at the time of writing. Exhibit 1: The signal from trimmed-mean inflation measures can vary widely based on the definition of the trim Core PCE (% y/y) vs. different types of trimmed-mean PCE inflation Source: BEA, Dallas Fed, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Trimmed-mean inflation has its positives… In his Fed Chair nomination hearing, Kevin Warsh argued that he preferred measures like Dallas Fed trimmed-mean PCE inflation to traditional core inflation, which excludes food and energy. In our view, the biggest strength about trimmed-mean measures is that they are agnostic on what to exclude. This makes them less volatile than the traditional core and in theory a better gauge of underlying inflation. Beyond this, Dallas Fed researchers suggest that their trimmed-mean measure is a better predictor of headline inflation than the traditional core, and that it better explains labor market slack. Though this latter point appears marginal (Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3). They have also noted that the distribution of inflation data across the underlying components has fatter tails than a normal distribution. They argue that trimming provides a better measure of the central tendency of the distribution than simply taking the mean (i.e., headline PCE) when the data are not normally distributed. 0 2 4 6 2018 2019 2020 2021

In slowing economic growth environments, investors generally prefer companies with secure balance sheets. Firms returning cash to shareholders generally outperform in the middle of the economic cycle. Seats in these elections were mostly last contested in 2022, when Labour, for example, recorded its second best ever result in London. One useful benchmark for assessing local election results is the National Equivalent Vote, which estimates how the local vote might have translated nationwide. In 2022, Labour's NEV was 25%. In last year's local elections, it was 19%, broadly aligned with Labour's national polling. A number of polls, MRPs and seat estimates have been published in recent weeks. BritainElects and the New Statesman, for example, estimate that Labour could retain 616 seats, out of the 2557 which they are contesting. This would be a loss of 1941 seats, potentially taking Labour to below 21.4% of councilors held after the 2009 elections. Oxford University's Professor Michael Thrasher has assessed Labour's possible losses as follows: "a good night for Labour is to limit losses to 800 seats (about a third of its total) and to lose control in only a handful of the more than sixty councils it is defending. 1,000 losses would be okay but as the number rises to 1,500...that’s close to the percentage of seat defeats Labour endured in 2025...Should Labour reach 2,000 losses or more that...would certainly mean the loss of councils that have had Labour- run administrations for 50 years or more". Rapid house price appreciation post-COVID and materially elevated mortgage rates since mid-2022 led to a significant decrease in first-time home buyers. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 11 Tax tracking: running just ahead of expectations The tax filing deadline for individuals, April 15, has come and gone, but the IRS still needs to process returns and people also file late, so we're continuing to track the daily data from the Treasury. We expected that individual tax refunds would be cumulatively ~$50-60 billion higher this year versus last, equivalent to a ~15% rise. Tracking has been broadly consistent with that projection. Top left, the total dollar amount of refunds issued by the IRS, including both electronic and checks, year-to-date totaled $330bn, ~$49bn or 17% ahead of the same point last year in data to May 6. Top right, the outflow from Treasury for electronically transferred refunds year-to-date, stood at $316bn, ~$59bn or 23% ahead of the same point last year in data to May 6. Typically, the cumulative flows tend to flatten out around this point in the tax filing season. In the latest weekly data from the IRS, see here, there was some catch up in filing and processing. The number of tax returns filed as of April 24 was down by 0.2% and the number processed was up by 0.4%. These lags in filing and processing widened as we approached tax day. The total amount refunded was up 18% according to that data with the average refund amount 11% higher. No let up from supply shocks A critical element of the optimistic view on the inflation outlook features a sharp reversal in core goods inflation as tariff -driven price pressures recede. We agree that this will eventually occur. However, the timing of the reversal is uncertain, and these price pressures could well persist for longer than expected. To gauge the magnitude and timing of tariff -driven inflation pressures, we have focused on measures of pipeline inflation from the PPI. In particular, the intermediate demand inputs stage 4 core goods series has shown to be a reasonably good leading indica tor for CPI core goods (ex cluding used cars) inflation during and since the pandemic. That data series, which leads CPI core goods ex used cars by 4 -5 months, remained elevated through the latest reading in March, consistent with higher consumer core goods inflation at least into Q3. Responses for this survey are typically collected within the first 10 to 12 days of the month and last year responses were collected from May 2 to May 9. Within that period this May, Brent crude oil prices reached $114.44 a barrel on May 4, compared to the $72.48 price on February 27 ahead of the geopolitical escalation on February 28. In the latest data available, Brent crude oil prices sat at $101 a barrel on May 8. Realized and expected fuel price increases likely weighed on the Empire State index in May, particularly in the outlook and prices components, and supply availability likely remained a drag after further deterioration in March and April. This leads to the creation of the credit rating slope, i.e., the amount of extra yield pickup that corresponds to a 1-notch differential between two countries. One could argue that this relationship shouldn't be linear (i.e., requiring higher compensation the closer we get to the sub-investment grade threshold), so we use exponential mapping. The residuals implied by this framework tend to be persistent (reflecting recent upgrade/downgrade momentum, as well as liquidity premia). More often than not, the market tends to be leading while credit ratings are adjusted with a lag. The result is tightening not only in crude balances, but increasingly in the availability of usable fuels like gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG and naphtha. This shift is already visible in prices. From January through April, crude prices have risen by roughly 40%, while refined product prices in Asia—the region hit hardest so far—have increased by 60% to 120%. Put differently, products are repricing 1.5x to 3x faster than crude and, to date, have shouldered twice the adjustment. This matters because consumers don’t buy crude oil—they buy fuels. Which leads to the next question: can crude remain broadly stable around current levels while refined product prices continue to rise? The answer appears to be yes—and that may well become the dominant adjustment mechanism. If refinery runs remain constrained by insufficient crude availability, the bottleneck shifts downstream. In that case, refined product prices—not another sharp leg higher in crude—become the primary transmission channel for demand destruction. In that scenario, crude could plausibly stabilize around $100 even as product cracks widen sharply. The next phase of the shock then may look less like a classic crude spike and more like a refining and end-user fuel crunch. The next question, therefore, is which products are most vulnerable. records.text: me inputs to the breakeven calculation are uncertain—the pace of n net immigration, the extent to which immigrant workers are captured by official statistics, and the path of the participation rate—we also consider a backward-looking approach that asks how many jobs would have been needed to stabilize the unemployment rate over the prior year. This approach, which implicitly assumes that last year’s trends will remain a good guide going forward, implies a breakeven rate of about 30k currently. While these breakeven estimates provide a benchmark for jobs needed to keep the unemployment rate stable, the actual number in a given month can be quite different due to monthly volatility in participation rate and other sampling issues. We find that the unemployment rate moves in the direction predicted by the difference that month between actual payroll growth and any given breakeven estimate only 60–70% of the time. As of March, our estimate of underlying trend job growth has rebounded to n about 50k per month, close to our estimate of the breakeven rate. Our forecast calls for job growth to slow this year, raising the unemployment rate by 0.3pp to 4.6%, though the recent resilience of the activity data have made the outlook more uncertain. records.text: M Idea 2 Aluminium Aluminium is expected to be in a large deficit in 2026… With our early April price deck, we modelled ~3 mtpa of Middle East smelting lost since the start of the Middle East conflict (>4% of global supply), driven by strikes and raw material shortages. Wood Mackenzie also estimates an additional 400-500 kt of output loss in Iran following a direct attack on one smelter as well as supply chain issues. This materially tightens an already constrained market, especially with South32’s 500 ktpa Mozal smelter also shutting in March. Restarts elsewhere look limited given still- challenging power costs. Indonesia remains the main source of growth, though ramp-up may be constrained by power availability. China’s capacity cap should limit expansion, although high margins may incentivise increased amperage, which can allow production to exceed capacity. We model 1.4% growth in global aluminium demand this year despite softer construction and solar demand in China. Energy storage systems are an increasingly important source of demand, with shipments expected to grow by 50% in 2026, driving a ~490 kt increase in aluminium demand. Together, these push aluminium to a near-record 1.85 Mt deficit, with further production at risk if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and the still-operating smelters start to run out of alumina. One critical issue in gauging the future direction of monetary policy will be whether these upside risks materialize. One set of data providing the clearest indication of this risk is the Japan Finance Corporation’s monthly small business survey. Despite limitations like a relatively small sample size and low response rate, it provides valuable insights for economic analysis thanks to its timeliness and availability of long-term data going back to 1974. The April survey (conducted in mid-April) reveals that the BoJ's concerns are indeed materializing. The sales price DI, an indicator of corporate pricing behavior, surged by 9.9 points MoM to 19.4, a level not seen since April 2023. Similarly, the input price DI, an indicator of cost pressures, jumped 26.0 points to 50.6, its highest reading since November 2022. LLC US Daily: The Breakeven Rate Debate: How Many Jobs Do We Need to Create? 7 May 2026 | 3:49PM EDT After falling into negative territory in 2025, payroll growth has rebounded in n recent months, and the unemployment rate has shown signs of stabilization. But with a somewhat weaker growth outlook, rising energy costs, and growing AI adoption likely to weigh on hiring this year, a key question is how many jobs we need each month to prevent further increases in unemployment. Combining our estimates of net immigration with Census projections of n native-born population growth and the CBO’s participation rate forecast, we estimate that the breakeven rate—the pace of job growth needed to keep the unemployment rate stable—will fall from 65k per month currently to 50k by year-end. Some estimates from Fed economists put the breakeven rate closer to zero in 2026, below our baseline, for two reasons. First, many of them rely on an estimate from Brookings that assumes net immigration will turn negative due to large voluntary departures. Second, some assume that recent declines in the participation rate—caused in part by the delayed incorporation of data from the 2020 Census—will continue at the same pace in 2026. records.text: seems justified against the current global inflation backdrop, the extent of the increase suggests some concern that the near-term policy path may be insufficient to temper inflation risks. Curve dynamics during the recent shock have resulted in the forward curve building in a bit more medium-term slope rather than pricing a discernibly faster pace of hikes. This contrasts with the rest of the G4, where markets have priced a more hawkish policy reaction to the inflation shock (Exhibit 2). The more aggressive repricing of US, UK, and European monetary policy expectations has limited the rise in long-end risk premia and prevented a more aggressive steepening of the curve. On a longer horizon, a large portion of the increase in long-end JGB yields can be attributed to a normalization in curve shape to pre-GFC levels, which our model picks up as higher term premium. Term premia estimates across the G4 have repriced higher, with Japan leading the recent adjustment (Exhibit 3). That said, recent long-end repricing has looked more out of step with markets’ expected path for policy and the rise in DM term premium. The common upward trend in the slope of the JGB curve and longer-term inflation pricing suggest greater concern that policy may be proceeding too gradually (Exhibit 4), as well as pricing potential risk of further fiscal loosening. records.text: Taking stock of sector performance In early April, we launched a comprehensive sector framework built around four key themes: (1) comfort with Financials in a slowing but non-recessionary growth backdrop; (2) a preference for heavy-asset sectors with lower technology obsolescence risk; (3) a bias toward commodity- and defense-linked sectors; and (4) underweights in energy-input-intensive sectors. Our key overweights include Banks, Insurance, Energy, and Aerospace & Defense. Key underweights include Automotive, REITs, and Food & Beverage. We are neutral on Technology, Wirelines, and Metals & Mining (among others). There has been some mean reversion following the March sell-off, although many of the top and bottom performers have been idiosyncratic. Cross-market themes include outperformance in Chemicals and Insurance alongside underperformance in energy-intensive and cyclical sectors such as Airlines and Construction Machinery. Growth and geopolitics are the key signposts to watch Our sector views are highly contingent on a macroeconomic backdrop of below-trend (but non-recessionary) growth, structurally elevated energy prices, and a somewhat more hawkish central bank reaction function from the ECB. The next several days are likely to be critical given the potential for (1) information related to a potential resolution to the Iran war and (2) insight into the health of the US labor market and, by extension, the broader economy (with the non-farm payrolls report on May 8). These doubts have intensified in recent months with accelerating inflation and stagnant economic activity. Our view is that they are unlikely to disappear without a shift in monetary policy, alongside eventual adjustments to the exchange-rate bands and the remaining capital controls. FX bands shift volatility toward interest rates: Under a monetary aggregates framework where the interest rate is endogenous, the volatility of rates is naturally higher. In Argentina’s current regime, which also features exchange rate bands with a ceiling that is not particularly high in real terms, the volatility of rates is even greater. If the goal is to reduce the variability in FX, that volatility is transferred to other variables – in this case, interest rates. It seems intuitive to assert that under this framework, interest rate volatility rises as the exchange rate moves further from the center of the band. Still, we do not think the Treasury is looking at this as a way to reduce interest expense. As the presenting member highlighted, there are several ways to define excess cash at the TGA. We think the best way to define excess is the amount in TGA that is above the next 5-day outflows. Now, to be clear, Treasury may not have a perfect measure of this ahead of time, and we think only a fraction of the ‘excess’ is likely to be invested in repo. For instance, the Treasury is unlikely to move >$100bn in and out of the repo market in a high frequency. Another potential definition of excess could be the amount above the current (quarterly) target. In Figure 6 we show how the excess has evolved over the past few years under the two definitions. We attributed some of the April NFP strength to the pandemic's undue influence on seasonal adjustment, which after looking through the details we still think is the case. The increase also got a boost relative to our expectations from the now-famous residual net birth death adjustment. Preceding months' gains were revised down -16K. Our assessment of the trend in nonfarm payroll employment of say ~50K jobs per month in the published data remains. That's not much different than the 3, 6, 8 month moving averages. The 4-month moving average is getting some help from the base effects (January strength undoing December weakness), and we expect that April likely revises lower in the next two reports, which has been the tendency in recent years. Note that assessment of the trend in the published data does not account for the monthly survey overstatement. For the FOMC, another decent month of job gains, nothing bad happening, and decent internals, reinforces the resilience theme. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 08 May 2026 11 If a leadership challenge were to occur, potentially higher spending can support growth but policy uncertainty and possibility of higher taxes or higher borrowing costs can offset some of it. It is worth noting that fiscal pressures are high, no matter who the Labour leader is. Even if there is no change in Labour leadership, there is likely to be fiscal pressure to provide support in response to the energy shock along with public services and defence spending pressures, which may increase further if Labour losses are large in the local elections. Risks of non- manifesto tax rises remain in coming years. Moreover, the move higher in yields along with potentially weaker growth or higher inflation is likely to have already hurt the headroom. Having said that, we don't expect the fiscal response to the energy shock to be as forceful as in 2022, given the limited fiscal space. Targeted temporary support to low-income households costing low single-digit billions looks more likely.

records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 Strong private payrolls, flat unemployment rate Payrolls rose solidly in April, with broad strength across goods and services employment. In goods, manufacturing inched down but only after a strong March; in services there were broad gains. Consumer-facing payrolls include strong retail and leisure payrolls. Business services rose, if only modestly. Healthcare payrolls carried on their strength. Finance payrolls fell, but only after a strong March. Information payrolls fell for a second straight month. The longer workweek also suggested ongoing labor demand. Payrolls and earnings Average hourly earnings rose only 0.16% but were up a decent 3.6% y/y. Given the pace of productivity growth, this pace of wage gains is not a source of inflation. Among production workers, aggregate hours rose 0.1% m/m and were up at a 1.1% annual rate versus the 1Q average. That's about the same as the 1Q pace and stronger than last year. On a 4Q/4Q basis last year, these aggregate hours rose 0.5%. Labor demand is still rising solidly. Aggregate payroll incomes rose solidly on the month with the combination of strong payrolls and a longer average workweek for all workers. records.text: EC noted that it intends to provide all the preliminary assessments by 20 November, and the EFC intends to provide its opinion on these by 8 December. This allows the EC to adopt the payment decisions by 18 December, allowing it to execute the final RRF payments by the 31 December deadline. The EU’s decision-making process, with the requirement of a unanimous decision on the budget, is the main obstacle for deferral of NGEU repayments. Whilst there is clearly a need – which could be argued to be partially self-inflicted by the EU countries’ inability to balance their budgets – and even perhaps the (short-term) economic rationale to defer NGEU repayments, the political and institutional hurdles to overcome are, whilst not insurmountable, still significant. The key obstacle is the requirement of unanimous decision on the EU budget and own resources decision, a point again proven by the temporary blocking of EU’s €90bn loan to Ukraine by Hungary. A deferral of NGEU repayments without a concrete plan is unlikely to be acceptable to fiscally conservative member states. As discussed above, a deferral of NGEU repayments would lower the burden on the next MFF, but this would come at the expense of the future MFFs. Vacant inventory build-up in mid-tier is persistent, with net deliveries elevated by over 90% versus 2019. In contrast, net deliveries for top-tier properties are now below pre-COVID levels. And indeed, consumption growth, supported by strong real wage gains, was one of the key growth drivers in the euro area in past years (1.5pp cumulatively in 2024 and 2025, i.e. 65% of EA growth). The energy shock directly affects that growth pillar, as higher inflation will reduce consumption growth, all else equal. This is the main reason we have lowered our growth forecast since the start of the Middle East conflict. The expected negative growth impact so far is limited and concentrated in 2026 - but it is increasing with the duration of the energy price shock and could become much larger (see here). A more subtle impact of the energy shock is that it takes away a potential driver of significant upside to growth, at least for some time: the elevated economic uncertainty is likely to be bad news for anyone who was banking on a boost to European growth from a fall in the savings rate. And this leads us to our topic of the day: the evolution of the euro area household savings rate. It currently stands at 14.4%, almost 2ppt above its pre-pandemic average. The savings rate increased strongly during the pandemic and then fell back to around 13% at the end of 2022. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 remains elevated relative to pre-pandemic norms, though layoff rates remain broadly stable, reinforcing the view that labor market softening continues to be driven more by weaker hiring than by widespread job losses. Youth unemployment rose further to 14.3%, remaining materially above pre-pandemic averages, while unemployment among core-aged men also increased. Population growth continues to decelerate sharply, with the LFS monthly population estimate slowing to 0.76% y/y in April from rates above 3% last year. The quarterly population survey—which we view as the more reliable measure of underlying demographic trends—has now turned negative on a sequential annualized basis. The divergence between the monthly and quarterly measures largely reflects methodological differences: the monthly population estimate is a model-based intercensal projection focused on the 15+ population, while the quarterly survey incorporates broader demographic benchmarking and migration updates that tend to provide a more stable estimate of underlying population dynamics. The result is tightening not only in crude balances, but increasingly in the availability of usable fuels like gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG and naphtha. This shift is already visible in prices. From January through April, crude prices have risen by roughly 40%, while refined product prices in Asia—the region hit hardest so far—have increased by 60% to 120%. Put differently, products are repricing 1.5x to 3x faster than crude and, to date, have shouldered twice the adjustment. This matters because consumers don’t buy crude oil—they buy fuels. Which leads to the next question: can crude remain broadly stable around current levels while refined product prices continue to rise? The answer appears to be yes—and that may well become the dominant adjustment mechanism. If refinery runs remain constrained by insufficient crude availability, the bottleneck shifts downstream. In that case, refined product prices—not another sharp leg higher in crude—become the primary transmission channel for demand destruction. In that scenario, crude could plausibly stabilize around $100 even as product cracks widen sharply. The next phase of the shock then may look less like a classic crude spike and more like a refining and end-user fuel crunch. The next question, therefore, is which products are most vulnerable. Two of the most prominent ones have been UK local elections and the new German budget. It’s all been about the potential fiscal implications of both events and whether they would justify higher yields. While both topics are subject to risks, we argue that we could end up with another case of "much ado about nothing". UK: leadership could be challenged, but would things really change? Several press articles have reported expectations of Labour losses in the local elections on 7 May. Such an outcome could increase the risk of a leadership challenge to the PM, though uncertainty on a clear alternative could delay any challenge. This has triggered questions from clients on what a new Labour leader would mean for economic policies and markets. The answer remains far from clear-cut and the end-point does not need to be very different from where we are today. Yes, in the event of a leadership challenge and potentially a more left-leaning Labour leader, market concerns could intensify around adherence to fiscal rules, with associated risks of higher borrowing and fiscal credibility. records.text: Without a more proactive approach from the BoJ or a reduction in fiscal risk and inflation uncertainty, we think risk premium in JGBs will remain intact. Our spillovers model suggests that most of the bearish impulse to JGBs has come from domestic drivers, with less than a third from abroad since the conflict began (Exhibit 9). While additional relief via lower global yields would be a small bullish impulse for JPY rates, the larger contribution from domestic factors means that any substantive moderation in long-end yields will have to come from domestic sources. The apparent MoF interventions in JPY reflect this challenge—neither BoJ policy nor global yields are sufficient to reduce pressure on the currency. However, while intervention “works” to buy time, ultimately only macro fundamentals can shift the trend, and those fundamentals are still pushing in the other direction. Our economists see inflation returning to a below-2% pace in Q4 2027 under their 1.5% terminal rate forecast, given that inflation expectations have remained well-anchored. But we think the market continues to look for reassurance that the BoJ is willing to respond to elevated inflation risks. Until that reassurance materializes, we think that the market will continue to retain higher risk premium. records.text: e increases in the TGA drain reserves from the banking system. This complicates reserve management for the Fed under the ample reserves framework. For example, this past April the TGA increased from roughly $700bn to over $1tn in the span of about a week. While no funding pressures emerged as reserves were drained, this dynamic was a concern for the Fed last December and one factor behind it initiating its RMP program at an elevated $40bn per month pace. Against that backdrop, several themes emerged from the TBAC discussion. The first is that the amount of excess TGA cash available to invest is subject to large swings. Some days Treasury might have hundreds of billions of excess cash, other days it might have none. Moving that excess cash in and out of repo means that repo markets would need to absorb potentially large and abrupt swings in Treasury cash flows. For this reason, TBAC noted that such an excess cash repo investment program would likely need to be capped. FIGURE 1. records.text: gh four channels: royalties, special participations, taxes paid by oil companies, and dividends from Petrobras. Royalties are financial compensations paid for the exploitation of oil and gas resources, calculated as a percentage of gross production value — directly proportional to oil prices and output volumes. Although royalties are shared across levels of government, historical data suggest that roughly 40% of revenues from the exploitation of natural resources accrue to the federal government. Special participations act as a quasi-windfall tax on highly productive oil fields, with progressive rates applied to net revenues. As a result, they are significantly more sensitive to oil prices and display non-linear behavior during price upswings. Importantly, special participations are more concentrated at the federal level than royalties, amplifying their relevance when prices rise persistently. Beyond these direct channels, higher oil prices also increase corporate tax revenues, notably corporate income tax (IRPJ) and the social contribution on net profits (CSLL), 60 80 100 120 Apr-25 Jun-25 Aug-25 Oct-25 Dec-25 Feb-26 Apr-26

records.text: the unchanged unemployment rate, April's data imply stronger gains in private payroll income than in February and March. Gains were seen in the workweek, which was up 0.1hrs, to 34.3hrs, while average hourly earnings slowed to 0.2% m/m (3.6% y/y). Taken together, the estimates imply a solid 0.6% m/m increase in private payroll income (Figure 7), compared with 0.2% m/m in February's report and 0.1% m/m in March's. Smoothing through the monthly swings, however, the 3m saar pace is 3.3%, barely enough to cover inflation. These income data seem broadly consistent with our outlook, which sees real consumer spending growth stepping down gradually, from 2.0% q/q saar in the current quarter to 1.0% by H2 26. The income gains that we do see derive mostly from wage growth and favorable changes in the composition of labor market income. According to our state-space model, which estimates the underlying pace of monthly wage gains using signals from AHE, the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker, and the Employment Cost Index, underlying wage gains amount to 0.24% m/m (2.9% saar), unchanged from our last estimate (Figure 9). The NEC, however, is not exclusively tied to a severe downturn but focuses on any exceptional circumstances outside the control of an individual member state likely to have a major impact on its public finances. National Escape Clause for defence spending: Last year, the Commission indicated it would authorize the NEC for all member states officially requesting it for defense expenditures. This is part of European Readiness 2030 (formerly the ReArm Europe Plan), which emphasizes the need for increased European investment, capabilities, coordination, and strategic foresight in defense, even with NATO's continued importance. The defence NEC together with the new SAFE facility represents the main EU tools supporting governments on defence spending. The plan aims to bolster the EU's external security and enhance its ability to deter and defend against aggression. The NEC for defense spending allows member states to increase defense expenditures by up to 1.5% of GDP annually until 2028 without triggering an EDP. The rationale is clear: new geopolitical tensions have fundamentally altered the pre-2022 global or der. This has created exceptional circumstances necessitating investment in strategic autonomy, including defense. This can be viewed as an external shock beyond member states' control. We expect 12-month core CPI inflation jumped up from 2.46% in February and 2.60% in March to 2.73% in April. A key driver of our April CPI projection is a double month of housing rents that combines both the April increase and the increase that should have been observed in last year's October CPI, but was set to zero due to the government shutdown. We expect very large increases in owners' equivalent rent (OER), the largest single component in the CPI, and tenants' rent (aka rent of primary residence) as they rebound from the government shutdown issues. Over the longer run the trend for CPI rent inflation continues to be downward with 12-month changes in new tenants' rents continuing to weaken. Core non-transportation goods prices continue to increase amid gradual tariff pass- through and are projected to have risen 0.14% in April — a bit below the pace of the past couple of months Information technology goods are projected to see the largest increases based on the Nielsen data and Adobe data we have in hand. Looking over the longer term, the 12-month change for core non-transportation goods prices is projected to have risen to 2.26% in April. Data as of May 01, 2026 Impact statements: Companies increasingly highlight that the energy shock is broadening across cost bases, with higher fuel prices flowing through freight, logistics, construction, claims, livestock, and a widening range of operational inputs. Importantly, the impact no longer remains confined to transport‑heavy industries, with retailers now seeing fuel‑driven inflation emerge across food supply chains and consumer goods. In response, mitigation efforts are becoming more internally focused. Banks are prioritising tighter cost control, capital discipline, working capital management, and productivity, while consumer‑facing businesses are accelerating automation, supplier negotiations, organisational streamlining, and inventory optimisation as they adapt to structurally higher operating costs. Less certain outlooks: Demand conditions are slowing, although increasingly in a two‑speed pattern. Consumer‑exposed sectors remain under the greatest pressure as households respond to elevated fuel and living costs by consolidating purchases, trading down, and relying more heavily on promotions and discounting outside key trading periods. Elsewhere, the slowdown appears more like a moderation, with housing and credit activity easing, while demand tied to infrastructure, energy, and AI/data centre investment remains comparatively resilient, supported by long‑dated project pipelines.

We also show the change in these residuals over the past 5/10/20 days to identify which spreads have been richening/cheapening lately. ompany. For Singapore, fuel pricing is fully liberalized, with pump prices adjusting in tandem with oil prices and operating cost dynamics. Singapore does not provide broad-based subsidies to households, as this would run counter to its long-standing “car-lite” policy objectives. Instead, support tends to be targeted at specific groups whose livelihoods may be affected by higher fuel costs, such as transport operators and drivers. For Philippines, support measures tend to be highly targeted at vulnerable groups. The government also coordinates with the oil industry to stagger pump price adjustments, so as to cushion the impact of higher oil prices on households. The New Zealand government opted against fuel tax cuts or price caps, instead implementing targeted household relief and fuel security measures. From 7 Apr 2026, the government introduced temporary weekly cash payments (around NZ$50) to approximately 150,000 low and middle income working families, delivered via an increase in the in-work tax credit. These mechanisms contain near-term inflation outcomes but tend to shift the burden to public finances or public-sector balance sheets. While energy subsidies and stabilization tools could help cushion the immediate inflation hit, fiscal costs can rise quickly during prolonged shocks. This mirrors patterns seen in past commodity shocks, where governments prioritized price stability at the cost of larger fiscal outlays. 1200 1400 1600 1800 2000 2200 Jan-25 Feb-25 Mar-25 Apr-

Price increases in airfares were if anything modest in March given the increase in jet fuel costs, but with further upside risks the longer costs stay elevated. But if anything, airfares in PPI have remained stronger than in CPI over the last four years, suggesting some buffer of higher revenues for airlines. This could keep airfares in PPI (and thus PCE inflation) more muted compared to stronger increases in CPI airfares. Other details of PPI data that matter for PCE should be more muted, such as modest increases in medical services prices. Falling equity prices over the month of March should also lead to a decline in portfolio management fees in April PPI (we are penciling in -4.5%MoM). This should correlate with softer core services prices in PPI overall. Of course, rebounding equity prices in April will have the opposite effect next month, substantially boosting May PPI/PCE. Importantly, we will also continue to watch PPI data for signs that higher energy, transportation, and other input costs are pushing up prices for goods broadly. But in April we are penciling in a modest 0.2% increase in core goods prices in PPI. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 20 CIT issues ruling on Section 122 tariffs, stops short of universal injunction In a 2 to 1 decision, a panel of judges at the Court of International Trade (CIT) sided with the plaintiffs in the "State of Oregon v. Trump" case deeming that the administration's use of Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a universal 10% tariff in February was illegal. The case was brought by 24 states and a small group of businesses. The order issued by the CIT directs the government to implement the injunction within 5 days and refund "Importer Plaintiffs" the section 122 tariffs paid with interest, see here. The ruling only found standing in the case for Importer Plaintiffs, those bringing the case who had evidence of paying tariffs under the proclamation. The Court did not issue a universal injunction, which means that the tariffs are not nullified in their entirety and the ruling from the CIT today only applies to "The State of Washington, Burlap and Barrel, Inc., and Basic Fun, Inc." with other plaintiffs claims dismissed. We would expect that the administration will move quickly to appeal the CIT ruling to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Norges Bank: earlier move than expected, we stick to a 4.25% peak Norges Bank surprised once again, hiking rates to 4.25% at the May meeting. It was clearly a very close call, but we thought a hike in June was marginally more likely than a hike in May. Our reading is that Norges Bank decided to hike out of concern that disappointing market expectations would have weakened NOK meaningfully, affecting the inflation path. records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 4 Next Week’s Highlights Key events in Canadian markets next week Wednesday, May 13, 1:30pm Summary of Deliberations The key new information from the April BoC decision was an openness among officials to change rates again even if activity evolves in line with their latest forecasts. Of course, Macklem outlined scenarios in which rates could move higher or lower, but it is not clear if small rate adjustments absent a new shock would be higher or lower. The summary of deliberations may help shed some light on how officials are viewing how policy rates should interact with a closing output gap in a scenario of few new risks. It may be that officials are expecting rates to return closer to the mid-point of the neutral range at some point, implying around 50bp of hikes. Officials may mention in this in meeting discussions. But a return to the mid-point of neutral in theory should not occur until the output gap has closed. In officials’ forecasts, growth runs as strong as potential this year and only runs stronger than potential next year, suggesting the output gap would not close until 2027 at the earliest. This is much later than markets pricing close to 50bp of hikes this year. And a consistent pattern in recent MPR updates has been that an expected closing of the output gap continues to be pushed out in BoC forecasts. Fear of high oil prices passing through to core inflation is already reflected in the rich payer skews, which we view to be overstretched. We are cautious that next week’s 10y refunding auction could face marginal headwind. Our updated gamma hedging analysis shows that hedging ahead of CPI would modestly improve the performance of short vol strategies. Signs of de-escalation and divided Fed favor carry trades Despite the continuing deadlock in the Middle East conflict, sentiments appear to have improved with both sides at least willing to avoid further escalation. Even though there is no clear off ramp yet for the conflict, markets have shown signs of de-escalation over the past week, with the worst-case tail risk now reduced somewhat. As we have noted recently (US Rates Weekly - Refunding, foreign takedown and FOMC takeaways), crude oil continues to drive the near-term intraday moves for various assets, and the pullback in the oil price this week has contributed to the recent widening in swap spreads and the decline in implied rates vol (Figure 4). 10y swap spread has widened by as much as 4bps over a 1wk rolling window, which represents one of the sharpest outperformance in Treasuries relative to swaps in recent years (Figure 5). Most of the downgrade activity has taken place intra-rating bucket at the notch level, with fairly balanced activity across BBs/Bs/CCCs of intra-ratings bucket downgrade actions (around $20bn per notch). Leveraged loans: Downgrade activity has been rampant for most of the past few years, but year-to-date, upgrade/downgrade flows have become more balanced. Still, at the sector level, downgrades have outpaced upgrades meaningfully since YE24 within media/entertainment, materials, telecom, and software/services. Investment grade: A sleepy start to the year Year to date, IG rating actions have been fairly lackluster. Upgrades from BBB to single-A are at their lowest run rate since 2015 outside of COVID (in par terms), with just $11.6bn of upgrades this year (Figure 1). Meanwhile, downgrades to BBB from single-A have also been remarkably low, with just $8bn of volume so far in 2026 (Figure 2). One large caveat to both of these figures, however, is that Honda (~$6.5bn of par) is captured in both numbers: it was downgraded to BBB in March before receiving a Fitch rating that brought it back to single-A in April. Therefore, excluding Honda, the numbers are even more muted versus history. That said, it’s worth emphasizing that the newly bicameral Congress with a majority of right-wing parties will be a key counterbalance to the proposed reforms. Polls are pointing to a tight race between Keiko Fujimori and Roberto Sanchez in the 7 June runoff. A poll conduct- ed by Ipsos and published by the newspaper Perú 21 reveals that if the runoff were held between Juntos por el Perú (San- chez) and Fuerza Popular (Fujimori), both candidates are tied in citizens’ voting intentions, with 38% support each. Howev- er, there is a sizable group (24% of those surveyed) that still has not decided who to vote for. In this particular scenario, 7% do not specify which candidate they would prefer, while 17% say they would cast a blank ballot. There is still some time until the second round on the 7 June and trends can change, especially accounting for the lower rejection rate with which Fujimori seems to be starting this cycle, relative to the past three runoffs that she has lost. Student loan delinquencies surged nearly 2 percentage points to 16.4% in Q4, the highest since the series began in 2004, reflecting the resumption of reporting after a pandemic pause. Five drivers of K-shaped spending The two-pace economy Clients have been focused on the divergence in consumer spending between lower- and higher-income households. According to BAC aggregated credit & debit card data, the “K” in spending opened up in late-’24/early-’25, has continued to date, and is most pronounced in discretionary sectors. In this report, we document five factors that have driven and will likely continue to exacerbate K-shaped spending dynamics. K-shaped balance sheets The evolution of both sides of household balance sheets in recent years has favored higher-income cohorts. In other words, the effective quality gap between notches grows as we migrate down the ratings scale. Encouragingly, we are seeing improvement in both BBB/BB and B loans. The BBB/BB downgrade/upgrade ratio (0.26x) is historically low, sitting at the 9th percentile at month-end. The B downgrade/upgrade ratio (1.00x, inclusive of B+, B, B-) is also low, but not quite as significant, at the 27th percentile. Breaking the ratio down by numerator and denominator, the BBB/BB segment is benefiting from both numerous upgrades and relatively scarce downgrades. The trailing three-month count of upgrades (19) is at the 92nd percentile since 2011. On the flip side, the trailing three-month count of downgrades (5) is at the 18th percentile. This shows that upgrades seem to be a more powerful force in driving the ratio lower. It is a slightly different story for B-rated loans. Trailing three-month upgrades are elevated relative to history, at the 88th percentile, but downgrades are more middling, sitting at the 62nd percentile. Therefore, while upgrades are contributing to the improving ratio, downgrades are frequent enough to prevent the ratio from reaching the stellar BBB/BB ratio. Figure 4. It is worth noting that fiscal pressures are high, no matter who the Labour leader is. Even if there is no change in Labour leadership, there is likely to be fiscal pressure to provide support in response to the energy shock along with public services and defence spending pressures, which may increase further if Labour losses are large in the local elections. Risks of non- manifesto tax rises remain in coming years. Moreover, the move higher in yields along with potentially weaker growth or higher inflation is likely to have already hurt the headroom. Although past episodes show that earmarking rules can be relaxed, doing so typically requires political capital and legislative changes. Moreover, higher oil prices often trigger policy responses aimed at mitigating the impact of costlier fuels on households and firms. Measures such as fuel tax relief, subsidies or targeted transfers tend to absorb part of the additional fiscal space created by oil revenues. As a result, improvements in headline primary balances are usually smaller than the gross revenue windfall would suggest. The policy reaction function can recycle oil revenues back into mitigation measures. The proposed PLP 114/2026 explicitly establishes a mechanism whereby tax waivers aimed at offsetting the energy shock can be compensated by extraordinary federal oil‑related revenues. This institutionalizes the link between higher oil prices and fuel price stabilization, rather than allowing all additional revenues to flow to the primary balance. While outright sales seemed to stop in March, it is not clear that has given way to outright buying (Exhibit 7). Our JGB curve models now suggest that the 10s30s slope has flattened to levels very close to fair value, while the 2s5s and 5s10s segments now look clearly steep to fundamentals (Exhibit 8). If elevated core goods inflation is entirely about tariffs, we should anticipate that category will revert much closer to pre-tariff inflation rates once one-time price increases are fully reflected. However, if elevated core goods inflation represents in part demand-driven pressures that could prove to be more persistent, that should moderate expectations for near-term disinflation from this category. The case for AI to exert a meaningful drag on inflation is reasonably straightforward. But there are countervailing forces to this narrative. In the near term at least, AI has triggered a substantial positive aggregate demand shock, as investment has surged in anything AI-related, including software, chips, computers and peripheral equipment, and data centers. These investments are competing with alternative demands for resources. The prior section showed how AI-related demand is likely already lifting prices for some components of the basket. In addition, AI is likely to represent an ongoing source of demand that could create bottlenecks and pri ce pressures in key points of the supply chain -- the spillover to higher electricity prices is most obvious.
