In a repricing regime, market partici- pants often anticipate changes in the ECB's reaction function through the front-end of the swap curve, and invoice swap spreads mechanically respond because swap rates move more than bond yields. In contrast, in a more classic flight-to-quality episode, spreads widen because bond yields richen aggressively on safe-haven demand and collateral scarcity dynamics show up in repo/funding. This matters because the recent widening impulse in the front end should not be over-inter- preted as “risk-off” in the traditional sense. Instead, it has been much closer to a policy- path/terminal-rate repricing channel , with spreads behaving like a low-beta duration proxy to ECB pricing—particularly in Schatz/Bobl, where the link to 1Yx1Y €STR is typi- cally the cleanest. That beta is now fading (Figure 12T h e b e t a o f G e r m a n s w a p s p r e a d s t o f r o n t - e n d € S T R i s n o w f a d i n g . . . ). The simplest way to frame this is: as the market’s distribution of near-term ECB outcomes narrows (i.e., fewer abrupt repricing episodes), the spread/yield relationship should become less dominant, and spreads should revert to being anchored by more stable fundamentals—funding conditions, collateral dynamics, and flow/ issuance. records.text: ab 8 May 2026 Global Research Japan Economic Comment Production disruptions concentrated in consumer goods Supplier delivery times and production outlook deteriorate in consumer goods Concerns over production disruptions driven by a naphtha shortage are now visible in macro data. In the April manufacturing PMI, supplier delivery times fell sharply from 48.0 in March to 36.3 in April (a lower reading indicates longer delivery times), the weakest level since the Great East Japan Earthquake in April 2011. Breakdowns in the finalised PMI released last Friday show that intermediate goods (-2.1pt to 49.6) and capital goods (+0.1pt to 51.0) were broadly stable, while consumer goods fell sharply (-8.0pt to 38.7), indicating that supply chain disruptions are concentrated in the consumer goods manufacturing sector. This pattern is corroborated by the Manufacturing Production Forecast Index released the same day. While overall production expectations for May point to increases in most categories, non-durable goods are projected to drop sharply by 11%. Although detailed breakdowns are unavailable, the decline likely reflects naphtha-related daily necessities (note that most semi-durables are classified as non- durables). Production weakness likely temporary amid alternative sourcing, oil stockpiles That said, the deterioration in production is likely to be temporary. records.text: is framework, interest rate volatility rises as the exchange rate moves further from the center of the band. Defending an FX band is equivalent to defending an interest rate differential (see Target zones and interest rate variability, 1989), and this has been clearly visible in Argentina while the band has been in place (Figure 1). Interest rate volatility has fallen sharply in recent months, partly because the central bank (BCRA) imposed a floor of 20% on the overnight rate. While the BCRA reintroduced a lending facility in recent weeks, this does not operate as a formal ceiling for the overnight rate because the facility’s rate is linked to the average market rate traded during the session. In practice, therefore, there’s still no conventional policy-rate corridor, even if the overnight rate cannot be considered fully endogenous. Our view is that the lack of clarity about monetary policy reflects the economic team’s preference for discretion, resulting in more freedom to contain the exchange rate. KEY MESSAGES The Argentine FX band’s low ceiling in real terms may keep expected interest-rate volatility elevated, in turn limiting the recovery in credit despite a more expansionary monetary stance. The current backdrop might require lower country risk to become less contractionary. records.text: between stabilized and overall vacancies for the top tier to narrow further, as tenants continue to prefer newly delivered construction. Overall vacancies increased by 0.2% y/y in 1Q26, while that for stabilized apartments grew 0.7%. Furthermore, landlords now have limited pricing power due to elevated vacancies and macroeconomic pressures limiting renters' ability to absorb higher rents. This has constrained rent growth over the past three years and has led to marginally negative rent growth in the past three quarters across top-tier properties (Figure 6), which have seen vacancies decline. While additional supply moderation should support some improvement in rent growth this year, we expect rents to remain flat, with a marginally positive growth bias. In light of higher vacancies and stagnant rents, we lower our NOI growth estimate for this year from around 3% to 1%. Lower expense growth has helped operators achieve positive NOI growth, despite increasing vacancy rates and stagnant rent. As per REIT commentary, y/y expense growth has subsided significantly in recent quarters compared with 2023. However, owners may have less room to cut expenses, and any increase in inflation can lead to higher expenses. Likewise, our equity colleagues do not anticipate a near-term positive inflection in sector fundamentals (see 1Q26 Multifamily & Single-Family REIT Preview). 8 May 2026 54 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Escalation aversion, for now

BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Exhibit 18: Professional & business services, construction and leisure & hospitality saw a slowdown in job growth last year Monthly job growth by sector (yearly average, SA, thous) Source: BLS, Haver Analytics BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Rising corporate profits also fuel a K-shaped economy Since the pandemic, national accounts data have been pointing to a sustained increase in productivity. If anything, that productivity boost seems to be piling as corporate profits, as labor income has been steadily falling as a share of US GDP. It remains to be seen whether wages and salaries recoup some of their lost ground relative to corporate profits. But for now, higher profits relative to wages which also lead to higher stock prices are yet another driver of a K-shaped economy. This is because higher-income consumers tend to be more exposed to higher profits through bonuses, stock-based compensation (Exhibit 19). records.text: Roundup of last week’s economic and policy events China The headline RatingDog China Services PMI (formerly the Caixin Services PMI) rose to n 52.6 in April from 52.1 in March, suggesting service sector activity picked up pace. Growth momentum in the hospitality sector moderated during the 2026 Labor Day n holiday, with domestic visits and revenue increasing by 3.6% and 2.9% year on year, respectively. The momentum could have been weighed on by rising transportation costs (on the back of higher global energy prices), adverse weather conditions in southern China, and traffic diversion from late-April spring breaks (which was promoted nationwide this year). Tourism revenue per head remained similar to the last Labor Day holiday and below the pre-pandemic level, pointing to still-subdued consumer spending power. Furthermore, cross-border travel growth momentum softened, primarily due to heightened airfare arising from the Middle East conflict. The key question for investors is not whether higher oil prices lift revenues (they do), but how durable is the fiscal space this creates once earmarking rules and compensatory policies are considered. Exhibit 16: Oil prices have soared with the Middle East conflict and have not returned to pre-war levels since Brent nearest future prices US$/bbl (C01 Comdty) Source: Bloomberg BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH How higher oil prices feed into federal revenues Brazil has steadily increased oil production over the past decade, strengthening the link between the oil cycle and public finances. For the federal government, higher oil prices translate into additional revenues mainly through four channels: royalties, special participations, taxes paid by oil companies, and dividends from Petrobras. Royalties are financial compensations paid for the exploitation of oil and gas resources

records.text: M Update 2 Several forces are at play here. First of all, (real) interest rates are higher today than they were before the pandemic and, paired with significant wealth inequality, this leads to larger interest rate incomes accruing to households with a lower propensity to consume. As a result, the savings rate increases (see here for the case of France and here for recent ECB research on the topic). Second, the overall economic uncertainty is likely higher today than it was before the pandemic. At first glance, this statement may sound counterintuitive, as the unemployment rate, a key metric to determine savings behaviour, is at an historical low in the euro area. But such a perspective is misleading. First, the recent lows in the unemployment rate are also a function of a slowdown in labour force growth in 2024 and 2025. As labour force growth continues to moderate, looking at the unemployment rate alone can lead to overstating the strength of the labour market. Second, next to the level, the expected direction of travel matters too. Labour markets are clearly weakening from here, see also the latest ECB CES on consumer expectations of the economic situation (here). And higher economic uncertainty can also flow out of an expectation of future higher taxes. records.text: yields. Crucially, diesel sits in the “middle distillate” range as jet fuel, meaning the two products compete for many of the same molecules inside the barrel. That overlap creates a direct tug-of-war in refinery output between jet fuel and diesel. And the flexibility is limited: most refiners can shift only about 2-5% of total output between the two. As a result, boosting jet fuel production is rarely “free”: it almost always comes at the expense of diesel supply. This is where the broader economic consequences begin to emerge. When a refinery adjusts its operations to prioritize jet fuel, it sets off a chain reaction across broader energy markets. The immediate casualty of higher jet yields is typically diesel. If jet yields increase, diesel volume drops almost proportionally. And because diesel sits at the center of global logistics—trucking, shipping, rail, agriculture and mining—even modest supply losses can ripple across the broader economy. Gasoline is somewhat more insulated because it comes from the lighter part of the barrel, but it is not immune. As refiners shift focus toward middle distillates like jet, they often redirect heavier streams away from crackers, tightening the feedstock for gasoline output. This likely helps explain why US gasoline prices are at $4.56/gal and why the risk of $5 gasoline can no longer be dismissed. We see two main risks to the trade: spreads shifting significantly lower, below levels before the Middle East conflict erupted in late February (for example towards the 50 bp level against Bunds), and/or BTPs trading significantly above OATs. We view this as unlikely. Based on current developments around the conflict, we do not expect spreads to breach pre-war lows and sustain it. Favour cautious expressions in this environment: While risk assets have rallied significantly on hopes of a peace deal, at the time of writing, the Strait of Hormuz remain s effectively closed. But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.1% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.2% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 4.1% and to remain above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. We expect headline inflation falls quickly next year, as oil retraces. But we project price levels at the end of next year to be above our prior forecast, capturing higher food inflation and some lasting impact on global supply chains. The surge in energy prices is likely to pass through to core inflation as well, with a lag. We now expect 4Q/4Q 2026 core PCE to come in at 3.2%, vs. 2.8% previously. Core inflation could reach 2.3% by end 2027. records.text: To assess whether dividends are typically reinvested, we looked at seasonality in foreign portfolio flows into equities on the basis that recurring sizeable inflows in big dividend months may suggest dividend earnings are typically reinvested. We also examined whether equity performance prior to dividend payments (in the month before key dividend payment months) has any bearing on the FX moves seen during the most relevant weeks (as we think past equity performance could influence sentiment to reinvest dividends). On the first point, we found little discernible pick-up in foreign flows into local equities around dividend months (Figure 6), suggesting no broad-based bias to reinvest dividend earnings across any market in Asia. The clearest exception may be in IDR in April, where we see a greater tendency for strong foreign inflows into local equities. As we observe no FX seasonality here in April – despite dividend payments being most concentrated in this month and considering the high foreign portion of JCI dividend payments – we think the inflows suggest a bias to reinvest. On the second point, we found that for the KRW and MYR, stronger local equity performance may increase appetite to reinvest dividends, as we found local currency performance in key dividend payment weeks was not as weak in such moments (Figure 3 on pages 7 and 11). Tech now accounts for 17% of non-financials (11% of corps), behind just consumer non-cyclicals, and out of all corps, ranks third, behind banks as well. Historically, there is precedent for larger sectors, with consumer non-cyclicals (2020) and communications (2002) both having reached 24% before. Such rapid sector growth tends to coincide with sector underperformance. Since the GFC, sectors that grow at least 1pp relative to their portion of non-financials in a year have widened 8bp during the growth year and another 3bp in the following one. When tech experienced a growth cycle in 2015-17, it net underperformed the non-financial index by 16bp. Hyperscalers alone now account for 3% of corporates in the Global Agg, doubling since October. The supply surge has not been a US-only story, with issuers tapping several currencies in order to fund their ambitious capex goals. As they are smaller markets, one issuance can (and has) make up a sizable portion of a currency's corporate IG market. AI and data center issuance is also affecting other sectors, eg, utilities, and other asset classes such as ABS, CMBS, private credit, etc. A key question is how investors will commingle risk across all asset classes, as this cross-asset issuance increases the correlation and single company risk across fixed income markets. Supplier delivery times are treated inversely: longer delivery times (below 50) are interpreted as reflecting stronger demand and mechanically lift the headline PMI. Structural reforms to the welfare state system and healthcare insurance regimes should come on top, and might not impact the federal budget per se, but household disposable income may be hit (EUR 16bn in savings are planned for next year). The problem: A EUR 30bn funding gap also needs closing in 2028E (or more if 2027 corrective measures don’t get implemented as now planned), and bigger ones thereafter. Absent a growth surprise (to the upside), budget negotiations are likely to continue exerting substantial stress on government stability. From a sentiment perspective, fiscal easing is starting to take too long to show. Tightening, coincident with an oil price shock, could become the dominant driver of sentiment (and ultimately private sector demand). Risks to the deficit trajectory are two-sided Risks to the deficit trajectory for 2026 and 2027 are two-sided: • Cyclical deterioration could weigh on both 2026 and 2027. As a ballpark, a 1% change in growth typically creates deficit room of c EUR 9bn under the fiscal rule. records.text: n this report. Payroll growth beat our above-consensus forecast, with only modest downward revisions (16k), reinforcing the view that March wasn’t a fluke. This was the first back-to-back payroll gain in a year, with private payrolls averaging a solid 86k so far this year, the strongest four-month pace since 2024. Job growth also broadened beyond education and health into trade and transport, leisure and hospitality, and construction, even if weather played some role in this. Most importantly, the u-rate held steady at 4.3%. Although the unrounded rate (4.337% vs 4.256% in Mar) ticked up, there are no clear signs of rising slack. What did we not like about this print? There were some areas of weakness, largely concentrated in the HH survey. LFPR edged down a tenth to 61.8%, driven by the 55+ cohort, while prime-age participation held steady, a reassuring offset. HH employment fell by 226k, the fourth consecutive decline, leading to a divergence from the establishment survey. However, this is not unusual and we tend to lean more heavily on the NFP signal when this occurs. The U6 rose to 8.2%, highest since ’21 and the unemployment duration increased as well, both worth monitoring. Overall, this reinforces the view that this was a solid but not hot jobs report. Wages not indicative of an inflationary labor market Another point of concern in the report was wages disappointing at 0.2% m/m. records.text: The AI investment boom has been the biggest driver of the shift in corporate spending patterns. Following last week’s reports, the consensus of analysts is now for the mega-cap US hyperscalers to spend $755 billion on capex in 2026, representing growth of +83% vs. 2025. This capex is estimated to reach 100% of cash flows from operations this year, leaving little room to return cash to shareholders without a drawdown of cash balances or large increase in debt. Accordingly, the hyperscalers cut buybacks by -64% year/year during Q1, and now allocate 20% of total spending to buybacks and dividends compared to an average of 34% from 2017-2022. Even outside of tech, S&P 500 companies have generally shifted toward investment spending and away from buybacks. The median S&P 500 company that has reported so far grew capex by +8% and buybacks by +2% in Q1 2026. Across sectors, buyback growth was strongest in Financials, with the median company in most sectors shrinking repurchase spending on a year/year basis. records.text: Marija Veitmane 08 May 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Is equity rally too fast? Graphics edition Has the equity rally moved too far, too fast? It’s the question we hear most—especially with little progress on the Iran war and oil still near $100. Understanding the key drivers helps frame the answer. In short, we keep coming back to the Tech TINA story (There Is No Alternative)—best seen in four charts. • Return concentration: 75% of the rally is driven by just 10 IT companies—contributing 10.5% of the S&P 500’s 14% gain since the 31 March trough (Figure 1) • Earnings concentration: Tech’s dominance is backed by exceptionally strong earnings and guidance (Figure 2). The rest of the US market is growing, but at a far slower pace, while earnings outside US look even weaker • Holdings concentration: Institutional investors are fuelling the rally, increasing equity allocations in April by the most they have since November 2020, with the bulk directed into Tech (Figure 3) o Other beneficiaries of this Technology rally have been Asian markets – Korean and Taiwan (Figure 4), while cyclical plays have seen outflows – Industrials and Materials sectors, as well as China, Japan and Europe Overall, April’s rally has been a concentrated, earnings-driven Tech trade, fully embraced by institutional investors—suggesting room to run. The increase in the unemployment rate reflected a 226k decline in employment—driven by a 204k decline in employment in the population aged 20-24— that was partially offset by a 92k decline in the size of the labor force. The labor force participation rate edged down 0.1pp to 61.8%. Household employment adjusted for methodological differences between the household and payrolls survey and for changes in the BLS’s population estimates increased by 118k in April. The U6 underemployment rate increased by 0.2pp to 8.2%, largely reflecting an increase in part-time workers for economic reasons (+459k, SA by GS). 3. Our estimate of the underlying pace of job growth now stands at 51k, close to our estimate of the breakeven pace of job growth needed to keep the unemployment rate stable. 4. Average hourly earnings increased 0.16% month over month in April, below expectations. The year-over-year rate increased by 0.06pp to 3.57%, roughly in line with our wage tracker (3.6%) and still below the rate we estimate is compatible with the Fed’s 2% inflation target. Wages for production and non-supervisory workers increased by 0.34% month over month or 3.67% from a year ago. records.text: Large dividend months* Bullish USDxxx seasonality evident in large dividend months** Notable dividend payment weeks in Q2 2026*** Other considerations that may impact dividend-driven FX seasonality KRW April, August Week 17 Weeks 14-17 KOSPI annual dividend payments as a percentage of GDP have near-doubled since 2015 in the wake of governance reforms – and USDKRW has shown more consistent bullishness in week 17 in recent years. This may suggest FX seasonality is becoming more apparent as dividend payments become more meaningful. That said, our analysis finds some evidence that KRW seasonality in week 17 is less apparent when local equities have performed well, which may reflect either an investor inclination to re-invest dividends when local equities perform well, or KRW’s high-beta credentials. TWD July–September Weeks 29, 33 Week 15 Taiwan has encouraged listed companies to start paying dividends on a quarterly or semi-annual basis, meaning January, April, July and October may become the key dividend payment months. There are also plans to allow direct USD dividend payments for foreign investors (MoneyUDN, 22 April). The latter in particular could diminish dividend-driven FX seasonality. Our analysis finds a pattern of stronger bullish USDTWD seasonality when local equities have performed well, perhaps reflecting investors hitting risk limits considering high foreign ownership of local stocks already, encouraging them to repatriate, rather than reinvest, dividend earnings.

Oil prices absorb enormous amounts of information with remarkable speed. That raises an important question: how should we interpret Brent averaging only about $100 in the two months since the war began despite the largest supply disruption on record? Rather than signaling complacency, the market may be acknowledging a harsher reality: a shock of this magnitude cannot be absorbed through the crude market alone. There is simply not enough elasticity on the crude side of the system. Instead, the adjustment is increasingly being pushed down the barrel—out of crude and into refined products. Crude shortages have already forced refiners across Asia and Europe to cut runs by 2.1 mbd in March and 3.8 mbd in April. At the same time, the market has also lost an estimated 4.7 mbd of refined product exports from the Middle East itself. The result is tightening not only in crude balances, but increasingly in the availability of usable fuels like gasoline, diesel

Pending home sales, which usually lead existing home sales by one or two months, suggest a modest rebound in April. The pending home sales index rose 1.5% over the month in March, indicating stronger contract signings that should have led to improved closings in April (with the usual lag and some cancellations). Mortgage rates also moderated in April, possibly easing affordability constraints on the margin. According to the Mortgage Bankers Association, the 30-year contract interest rate was 6.51% in the week ending April 3, fell to 6.37% by the week ending April 24, but backed up slightly to 6.45% in the week ending May 1. Weak sales in March appeared to reflect stretched affordability — the National Association of Realtors' housing affordability index fell 3.8 points to 113.7 in March, and the level remains noticeably down from the ~160 average in the five years prior to the pandemic. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 52 Survey of Professional Forecasters (Q2), 10:00 AM The Survey of Professional Forecasters represents another read on inflation expectations for the FOMC. In the nearer term, in the Q1 survey forecasters left unchanged expectations for core PCE inflation in 2026 (2.7% Q4/Q4) and 2027 (2.3% Q4/Q4).  Upside: If long-term inflation expectations in the Q2 Survey of Professional Forecasters take a meaningful leg higher, it could raise the FOMC's concerns about inflation expectations remaining well-anchored amidst energy-driven cost pressures and ongoing geopolitical and policy uncertainty. FOMC communications consistently characterize long-term inflation expectations as well-anchored. For example, in the April press conference, Chair Powell said, " Near-term measures of inflation expectations have risen this year, likely because of the substantial rise in oil prices. Most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal."  Downside: Steadiness or a tick down in long-term inflation expectations would add another data point to the FOMC's view that inflation expectations remain well-anchored beyond the short term. Greater uncertainty around the path of short-term rates tends to widen lending-deposit spreads, as banks become more cautious in extending credit. The current setup may become harder to sustain: We argue that overall, design limitations in the FX band and monetary policy make an economic recovery less likely. Although the central bank is pursuing a more expansionary monetary stance, the transmission of that policy to credit is hampered by expected higher interest- rate volatility. When the exchange rate moves further from the center of the band, preventing interest-rate volatility from returning would be difficult. And given the band’s calibration (with a ceiling that is not an overshooting level in real terms, Figure 4), we believe FX is likely to remain between the band’s center and upper limit. On page 3, we discuss possible paths if the above does not hold. But if our hypothesis is correct, with a more expansionary BCRA stance failing to improve credit and economic recovery being delayed, the government will probably need to embark on a new phase in the stabilization program: i) Redefine monetary policy instruments and objectives; ii) Modify or scrap the exchange rate band regime; iii) Lift the remaining capital controls. Still, EUR appears relatively insensitive to ECB hike pricing. This likely reflects the fact that rate hikes in response to bad (inflation) reasons are typically less supportive than those in response to good (growth) reasons, even when well-calibrated – this is why a balanced ECB approach remains the ‘sweet spot’ for EUR. EUR resilience may also partly reflect relatively “well-behaved” European gas prices, which matter more for EUR crosses than Brent (see also EUR Watch 18 Mar '26). Stay cautious on EUR for now Where to from here? While our medium-term EUR bias is positive, we still see energy markets as priced to perfection and stay cautious in the near term (see Liquid Insight 5 May '26). First of all, (real) interest rates are higher today than they were before the pandemic and, paired with significant wealth inequality, this leads to larger interest rate incomes accruing to households with a lower propensity to consume. As a result, the savings rate increases (see here for the case of France and here for recent ECB research on the topic). Second, the overall economic uncertainty is likely higher today than it was before the pandemic. At first glance, this statement may sound counterintuitive, as the unemployment rate, a key metric to determine savings behaviour, is at an historical low in the euro area. But such a perspective is misleading. First, the recent lows in the unemployment rate are also a function of a slowdown in labour force growth in 2024 and 2025. As labour force growth continues to moderate, looking at the unemployment rate alone can lead to overstating the strength of the labour market. Second, next to the level, the expected direction of travel matters too. Labour markets are clearly weakening from here, see also the latest ECB CES on consumer expectations of the economic situation (here). And higher economic uncertainty can also flow out of an expectation of future higher taxes. Coastal versus Sun Belt Another factor that has garnered much attention is the performance difference between the Sun Belt and coastal regions. Since 2022, inventory across major CMBS Sun Belt markets has expanded by approximately 15%, compared with 7% growth in coastal markets and 10% nationally. This elevated construction continues to weigh on performance in the Sun Belt (Figure 11). Heavier supply in the Sun Belt has resulted in elevated vacancy rates, averaging 11.3%, versus 6.1% in coastal regions. This divergence is also evident in rent performance, with coastal markets delivering rent growth roughly 0.5pp above the national level while Sun Belt rents have underperformed the national level by approximately 2.5pp. We expect the prior overbuilding to continue to weigh on performance, although this risk is now well understood by CRE participants. One notable exception to this trend is Miami. While it is often grouped with the Sun Belt market, it is coastal by geography and is more luxury oriented. records.text: Pushing Back Fed Cuts to December and March We are pushing back the final two 25bp Fed rate cuts in our forecast by one quarter to December 2026 and March 2027, from September and December 2026 previously. Energy cost passthrough and other effects of the Iran war, as well as the (overstated) effects of AI demand on consumer prices, are likely to keep year-over-year core PCE inflation closer to 3% than 2% all year, as shown in Exhibit 1. Even before the war, many FOMC participants had already made it clear that they wanted to see inflation—the official rate, not the estimated rate excluding tariff effects that the leadership has cited—fall closer to the 2% target before resuming rate cuts. A higher inflation path will likely expand that group. As a result, we think that a combination of lower monthly inflation prints after the oil shock fades and further labor market softening will likely be needed for the FOMC to cut in 2026. We still expect that bar to be met but now expect it to take a bit longer. On the inflation side, we expect the path of month-on-month core PCE inflation to fall sharply in the second half of 2026 to a sub-2% annualized rate as the effects of tariffs and energy price passthrough fade, as shown on the left side of Exhibit 1. President Trump announced an imminent deal and the market, once again, rallied on the news and the prospects of a swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. We have been here many times before. And there is significant noise regarding what has been achieved so far, as well as uncertainty about the shape of the cost and benefit functions of the relevant parties in the war. However, an undeniable fact is that the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed for all practical purposes despite all the “imminent deals” in the making. As we discussed in our previous report ( Global Economic Weekly: Schrodinger’s Strait 24 April 2026), when the costs and benefits are private information for each party involved, every round of the war reveals how tough or weak each party is perceived by the other. records.text: New issue trends and sector performance Market participants have been especially focused on new issue trends as of late, driven by two key factors. First is the typical seasonal pattern. Over the course of the past 15 years, May ranks as one of the most active months for new issue activity as firms tackle financing needs in the period between 1Q earnings releases and the summer lull. Second is the recent acceleration of the AI-related wave of financing, which has been evident across a range of financing channels (liquid and private), innovative structures, and currencies. As we head into what will likely be an active month, we take stock of the year-to-date (YTD) IG and HY new issue activity in the USD and EUR markets. We see five notable takeaways related to (1) pace, (2) deal sizes, (3) sector leadership, (4) regional overlap, and (5) ratings. The pace: A strong start in IG, more mixed in HY YTD IG gross issuance—in both the USD and EUR markets—is very elevated (Exhibit 1). USD IG supply of $921 billion is well above the pace of the past few years and is essentially on par with 2020’s previous record level ($925 billion). YTD issuance in the EUR IG market of €339 billion has reached a new record (and is up 12% vs. this time in 2025). In the HY market, the backdrop is more mixed across regions. records.text: Improvements in energy efficiency boost economic growth over a slightly longer-term horizon via productivity gains. Improvements in energy efficiency will likely continue to support the growth of the Japanese economy. Our analysis above suggests that a channel has been in effect since 2000 whereby improvements in energy efficiency, spurred by rising crude oil prices, have a positive impact on economic growth via an increase in labor productivity. In this context, we conducted a VAR analysis to quantitatively grasp the impact of energy efficiency improvements on the growth rate over a slightly longer-term horizon. The results show that a 1% improvement in energy efficiency has the potential to lift the economic growth rate by about 0.1 to 0.2 pp over the following several years (Exhibit 8). Amid the shift from a deflationary to a reflationary economy, Japanese companies have been generating historically high corporate profits and taken an aggressive capex stance. Under these circumstances, many companies cite decarbonization as one of the drivers of capex. As such, it is likely that capex aimed at improving energy efficiency will continue to increase in the future (Exhibit 9). Export boom in China shows pain threshold still far away As we approach the Trump-Xi meeting, China continues showing signs of resilience. Despite conventional wisdom that China, being the biggest oil importer, would be hurt by the Iran war, no sign of significant pain is showing yet. Second, the currency is expensive, which we previously expected NBR to only attempt to address after headline inflation falls. NBR historically maintained about 2-3% RON depreciation vs. EUR per year to prevent loss of competitive- ness. In the five-year period 2017-2021, RON depreciated about 10% vs. EUR while the REER stayed stable. However, when inflation rates increased following Covid, NBR aban- doned this practice not to add FX passthrough to inflation. This resulted in a sharp real appreciation of the RON. But we continue to expect slowing monthly inflation data and clearer weakening in labor market data in the second half of the year will have officials cutting rates again in September. Historically, the monthly establishment survey has been a more stable indicator of employment trends compared to the household survey. Job growth averaging around 50k per month would presumably suggest a retightening labor market given market and Fed officials’ view that a breakeven pace of employment is much lower this year compared to previous years due to immigration changes (close to 0k). But we are cautious that the last 6 months are a time of year where lower average hiring has generally resulted in stronger seasonally adjusted payroll data. We continue to think that a labor market defined by low hiring will result in weaker data into the summer months. The unemployment rate remains the most important part of monthly employment data, and an (unrounded) increase in April despite a decline in labor force participation does not suggest a retightening of the labor market. Softer wage growth the last few months also does not suggest a retightening of the labor market that would necessitate rate hikes. records.text: Since 2000, the manufacturing sector, especially processing industries, has enhanced its energy efficiency. Improvements in energy efficiency have led to an increase in the capital-labor ratio and a rise in TFP , supporting labor productivity growth. The improvement in energy efficiency since 2000 has been brought about in particular by improvements in energy efficiency in the manufacturing sector (Exhibit 4).2 In considering the future performance of the Japanese economy, a key issue is whether these sustained improvements in energy efficiency will boost labor productivity. Labor productivity is known to depend on the capital-labor ratio and total factor productivity (TFP). Therefore, improvements in energy efficiency are thought to promote a rise in labor productivity if they (1) increase the capital-labor ratio through a rise in energy-saving capital stock and (2) raise TFP through improvements in production and operational processes. Accordingly, we examine the relationship between energy efficiency, the capital-labor ratio, and TFP . First, using macro data, we find a relationship where improvements in energy efficiency resulting from higher crude oil prices lead to increases in the capital-labor ratio and TFP . records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 16 The workweek rose 0.1 hours to 34.3 in April. On an unrounded basis, the workweek was up 0.06 from 34.224 to 34.281 in April. Generally the workweek has been relatively subdued. We think the workweek is one of the most important indicators in the labor market just now. This should help parse supply drivers from demand -- a rising workweek would be a sign that the stock effects from weaker immigration flows are potentially starting to lead to longer workweeks for existing workers. Within the industry detail, construction (+9) and leisure and hospitality (+14K) posted ok gains but not so strong weather support was obvious. Manufacturing employment swung back to a loss (-2K) , but the trend has improved, not surprisingly since output has risen over the past year. Temp help climbed 8K, punctuating a lot of weakness the past year. And as noted above, odd, outsized strength materialized in transportation and warehousing (30K). Retail employment climbed 22K in April, likely not the new trend, but helped by the early start to spring and summer. Government employment fell -8K, with the federal government falling 9K, and state and local government continuing their cooling trend, now closer to flatlining on net. The energy shock led to a clear divergence from previous forecasts , and market expectations have already begun to deteriorate. Market participant surveys currently show expectations for December 2026 inflation of around 27.5%, suggesting a roughly 6.5pp gap above the CBRT’s upper bound. We expect at least a 300–400bp upward revision in the CBRT’s inflation report next week. High for longer: The CBRT kept its policy rate at 37.0% at its April meeting, saying it will be monitoring potential second-round effects on inflation from recent oil price hikes. The central bank currently funds the market via the overnight lending rate, which is now at 40.0%, and we think the first-order strategy here is to keep funding rates elevated until geopolitical conditions ease. Easing cycle postponed to year end: We delay the expected start of the rate-cutting cycle from Q3 to Q4 2026 due to materially higher year-end inflation expectations and growing (upside) risks to the inflation outlook (year-end policy rate at 35% from 33% seen previously). records.text: What does all of this mean for the outlook for the unemployment rate? As of March, our estimate of underlying trend job growth has rebounded to about 50k per month, roughly in line with our breakeven rate estimate. But job growth was well below breakeven for most of the past year, the large energy cost shock from the recent Iran war will likely lower final demand growth and could make companies more reluctant to hire, and AI will likely become a more meaningful headwind to employment over the course of the year. For these reasons, our best guess is that the labor market will soften somewhat further this year, with the unemployment rate rising 0.3pp to 4.6% by year-end, though the recent resilience of the activity data have made the outlook more uncertain. While the Strait’s closure has removed a broad spectrum of refinery feedstock and refined product supplies, jet fuel has been most acutely affected. Jet prices have nearly doubled across Asia, Europe and the US, with jet cracks widening to an extraordinary $80-100 per barrel over crude. “Crack spreads” may sound esoteric, but the concept is straightforward: they approximate the margin refiners earn by turning crude into fuels—the difference between the price of crude and the value of the finished products produced from it. In practice, it’s the market’s way of telling refiners what to maximize. Right now, the signal is clear: produce as much jet fuel as possible. records.text: ab 8 May 2026 Global Research US Economics Weekly Inflation week up next Economic Comment: why is labor's share of income so low? The BLS reported labor's share fell to an all-time low in 2026Q1. The academic literature proposes a number of reasons for the post 1990s decline in labor's share. One theme that runs through most of those reasons is a lack of wage bargaining power for employees. The pandemic offered a glimpse of nominal wage inflation and demand for workers putting employees in the driver's seat but since late 2024 the prior trends have reasserted themselves. The labor market has generally slackened. Incoming nominal wage data has been on the soft side. How one thinks about wage bargaining has implications for how one thinks about inflation, the impact of the potential disruption, and what higher prices might do to erode real incomes and keep the affordability theme central to our politics. The Economic Comment begins on page 3. Our updated payroll employment indicator is on page 10. The Week Ahead: inflation week We expect the headline CPI rose 0.59% and the core CPI rose 0.37% in April, pushing 12-month rates to 3.76% and 2.73%, respectively. Rising gasoline prices likely boosted headline CPI, while owners' equivalent rent and tenants' rent probably saw strong gains in April as the bias from last fall’s government shutdown was unwound. See Alan's preview here and an update here. Together with PPI and import price data, the CPI will help refine our April core PCE

We think that risks remain skewed more towards ongoing closure of the Strait and potential escalation rather than a quick and clear path to resolution. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 49 Recall that retail sales are measured in nominal terms, and in the coming months could be boosted by increased energy costs, as well as any efforts by retailers to pass tariff- related price increases on to consumers. Special questions from the FRB of Kansas City manufacturing survey in April suggested limited pass-through of energy cost increases thus far, with over two-thirds of firms reporting that they were passing on 0-20% of increased costs (link here). However, ongoing margin compression if high energy prices persist could change firms' calculus. On tariffs, the Federal Reserve's Beige Book suggested firms are now raising prices after waiting to do so, but the extent of pass- through varies (link here).  Upside: The implications of a stronger-than-expected April headline retail sales figure would depend on the driver. Another broad based increase in sales would potentially signal households are weathering the rise in gasoline prices more readily and perhaps imply stronger momentum in spending. However, a larger-than-expected boost from sales at gasoline stations while sales at other stores are weaker would have less positive implications for the go-forward.  Downside: Disappointing April retail sales data could suggest that households pulled back on discretionary spending despite tax-refund support. This could potentially reflect higher gasoline prices crowding out spending in other areas and would imply softer consumption momentum

They do not run a fully fixed-price system, but governments actively smooth retail fuel pricing to protect households and damp near-term inflation volatility, especially during oil shocks. The key difference across this group is where the shock is absorbed first, whether it is the fund dedicated for oil price stabilization, or by state-owned oil enterprises. Source: Barclays Research Source: Barclays Research Our input-output analysis suggests, for example, that if crude oil imports decline by 50% and the shortfall cannot be covered by alternative procurement, GDP could contract by more than 2% ( Figure 5). This would be far larger than the impact from the terms-of-trade deterioration incorporated in our current forecast. In practice, however, supply constraints are likely to exert an earlier impact in the case of petroleum products, especially naphtha, than in the case of crude oil, where stockpiles are relatively ample. While the impact would be smaller than in a scenario where crude oil imports themselves decline, it is not negligible ( Figure 4). Similarly, there are potential nonlinear upside risks to inflation. As the BoJ emphasized in its 28 April Outlook Report, in recent years firms have become accustomed to raising prices and have become less hesitant to pass through not only cost increases stemming from external shocks such as higher oil prices, but also those associated with wage hikes. When crude oil prices rise, cost increases propagate downstream through the supply chain, and a high pass-through rate amplifies this effect. records.text: mics. As a major energy exporter, the US is more resilient against higher energy costs than its peers, reducing pressure on the Fed to shift toward rate hikes in the near term. In contrast, most G10 countries have either raised rates or are expected to do so soon. This monetary policy disparity, along with aggressive USD selling, leads us to be medium-term bearish on the dollar. To express this view, we decide to retain our long NZDUSD position and substitute our short EURNOK position with a short USDNOK position. These trades provide not only short exposure to the dollar but also commodity exposure, which we anticipate will perform favourably. Furthermore, we continue to maintain our long position in CADCHF for comparable reasons. At the same time, we see the GBP as particularly vulnerable in the short term. The UK's ability to withstand interest rate hikes is quite limited, making it an outlier compared to its 2026 growth forecast. While the economy clearly needed rate cuts this year, it may soon face the opposite situation. Therefore, we continue to have two short positions on GBP, paired against both the NZD and the JPY, where media reports continue to speculate on supportive intervention. records.text: yields. Crucially, diesel sits in the “middle distillate” range as jet fuel, meaning the two products compete for many of the same molecules inside the barrel. That overlap creates a direct tug-of-war in refinery output between jet fuel and diesel. And the flexibility is limited: most refiners can shift only about 2-5% of total output between the two. As a result, boosting jet fuel production is rarely “free”: it almost always comes at the expense of diesel supply. This is where the broader economic consequences begin to emerge. When a refinery adjusts its operations to prioritize jet fuel, it sets off a chain reaction across broader energy markets. The immediate casualty of higher jet yields is typically diesel. If jet yields increase, diesel volume drops almost proportionally. And because diesel sits at the center of global logistics—trucking, shipping, rail, agriculture and mining—even modest supply losses can ripple across the broader economy. Gasoline is somewhat more insulated because it comes from the lighter part of the barrel, but it is not immune. As refiners shift focus toward middle distillates like jet, they often redirect heavier streams away from crackers, tightening the feedstock for gasoline output. This likely helps explain why US gasoline prices are at $4.56/gal and why the risk of $5 gasoline can no longer be dismissed. records.text: Positive earnings revisions continue to lift the S&P 500 to new record highs. n Q1 earnings results have been strong, with year/year EPS growth for the S&P 500 tracking at +17%, excluding some one-time items. The S&P 500 has risen by +8% YTD alongside +13% growth in 12-month forward EPS estimates and a -4% decline in the P/E multiple. In addition to strong earnings growth, the Q1 reporting season has n demonstrated the ongoing shift in corporate spending priorities to capex from buybacks. S&P 500 companies have reported year/year capex growth of +38% so far in Q1 2026 vs. just +1% for buybacks. Our updated cash spending forecasts imply a continuation of that trend, with capex in 2026 growing by +33% to $2 trillion while buybacks grow just +3% to $1 trillion. This rotation has been driven primarily by the AI hyperscalers, which are expected to spend $755 billion on capex in 2026, but the same general trend is evident in most sectors. Investors have recently rewarded companies investing for growth over n companies returning cash to shareholders. They also appear to have halted their rotation toward weak balance sheet firms. The preference for growth investment spending has been apparent across industries but has been most pronounced in the AI complex. At the same time, the impact of the war on the outlooks for economic growth and Fed policy has put an end to the equity market rotation away from “quality” that defined much of 2025. records.text: Capex and R&D We forecast S&P 500 capex will grow by +33% in 2026 and +22% in 2027, driven primarily by the AI hyperscalers. The five largest AI hyperscalers – AMZN, GOOGL, META, MSFT, ORCL – accounted for 32% of S&P 500 capex in 2025. We separately estimate nominal capex for the hyperscalers, the S&P 500 Energy sector, and the S&P 500 ex-Energy to arrive at our aggregate S&P 500 capex forecast. Excluding Energy and AI hyperscalers, we forecast capex will grow by +9% in 2026 and +8% in 2027. We model capex growth as a function of earnings growth, policy uncertainty, and financial conditions. Solid earnings growth and easy financial conditions will more than offset elevated policy uncertainty. The index will also benefit from secular investments in power even excluding Energy and the AI hyperscalers. During 1Q earnings season, the median S&P 500 company grew capex by +8% year/year. Our economists’ capex tracker also points to solid growth, with the soft data component at +5% and the hard data component at +7% during April. Consensus expects Energy capex growth will be relatively muted, but the recent rise in energy prices could lead to a capex response in 2027 and beyond. On the back of higher oil prices, analysts have revised Energy cash flows higher. However, their estimates imply the benefit will be relatively short-lived. records.text: US Rates Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 14 underpricing the pass-through into core goods inflation from higher oil prices. Markets seem to be worried about the impact of oil prices on petrochemicals (plastics, rubber, etc.) which can feed directly into core goods inflation. While that does make sense theoretically, empirical evidence suggests otherwise. Historically, we have seen limited evidence that higher plastic prices will lead to higher CPI core goods inflation (Figure 22). Another factor that could limit pass-through into final prices is that while goods prices have continued to increase since the pandemic, plastic prices have declined (Figure 23). So, if plastic prices move slightly higher, producers should be able to absorb some of the additional costs. We thus find it hard to expect a significant increase in goods inflation due to higher energy prices. Figure 22. Higher plastic input costs have not always resulted in higher goods prices to the consumer Figure 23. Plastic prices are far lower than where they were a decade ago. So, it is hard to argue that an increase from these levels will directly lead to higher goods prices © 2026 Citigroup Inc. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 08 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Focus on credit risk has ramped meaningfully in recent quarters given the market’s growing concern with idiosyncratic and sector-specific headwinds. Software is top of mind, but it is not the only sore spot. The percentage of the Citi Leveraged Loan Tracker marked below $85 has risen to 4.2% in May, down from the 5.1% peak in March but still up from 2.8% at year-end. The last time the stressed segment was this large was in late 2023, when the market was still recovering from the Fed’s rate hike cycle. At that time, healthcare and telecom & cable loans were well represented in stress/distress versus today where nearly half of stress/distress are software loans. From a rating agency perspective, however, quality is improving. As we mentioned in our April Loan Dashboard, the trailing three-month downgrade/upgrade ratio slipped to 0.69 at month-end, the lowest in four years. records.text: most from the tech boom The outlook for the global economy depends heavily on whether the Strait of Hormuz opens. But the range of out- comes vary as we see two powerful forces driving economic activity. The first is a robust cyclical bounce owing to fading business caution, supportive fiscal policies, and the impact of the global easing cycle that began in 2024. The second force is the conflict in the Middle East that has generated a surge in energy prices. Absent an opening in the Strait of Hormuz, the global economy will feel the drag of the largest oil supply shock on record as inventory buffers dwindle and operational stress at producers intensifies (Figure 1). For now, the cycle is dominating, as underscored by this week’s US payroll report showing solid job growth over the two months since the start of hostilities. -4 -2 0 2 4 6 8 -16 -12 -8 -4 0 4 8 12 74 78 82 86 90 94 98 02 06 10 14 18 22 26 %oya, both scales (2Q26 fcst boxed, 10mbd prod. loss) Source: EIA, Rystad, J.P. Banxico currently sees ample economic slack (−2.1% of potential GDP, Figure 2). Overall, we expect the hiking premium embedded in the short end of the TIIE-F curve to be reduced. At its latest meeting, Banxico said its current monetary policy stance can cope with challenges arising from the Middle East conflict. This pushed the bar for near-term rate rises higher, in our view. Our base case still anticipates an additional 25bp cut, bringing the policy rate to 6.50%, and then a hold lasting for several quarters. The market, however, is pricing roughly 160bp of rate hikes over a two-year horizon. Such a gap makes front-end receivers attractive, assuming rates converge toward our forecast. Gasoline and other energy commodities prices are expected to have risen 6% in the April CPI, and other non-core prices, such as food at home, are also expected to have risen solidly. Next week's inflation reading should also be the first unbiased 12-month change since the shutdown in fall 2025, and we expect very large increases in owners' equivalent rent (OER) and tenants' rent as they rebound from the government shutdown issues. Together with the April PPI and import price data due out next week, CPI data will refine our April core PCE projection, which currently sits at 0.25%, leaving the 12-month core PCE inflation rate up 7 bps to 3.27%. Nominal sales at the control group of stores — which feed directly into the BEA's estimate of goods spending — are projected to have risen 0.4% in April, with support from bumper tax refunds and inflation. Since retail sales are measured in nominal terms, sales at gasoline stores likely boosted headline sales. We expect the Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit to show rising household debt balances and elevated delinquency rates in Q1, especially among low-income borrowers. Although private credit and broadly syndicated loans are not perfect substitutes, we believe there is significant overlap between the two universes and therefore are comfortable extending trends in one market to the other. Refining is essentially the process of separating a barrel of crude into different products according to boiling points. Gasoline, jet fuel and diesel represent the three dominant fuels produced from a barrel of oil. While modern refiners have some flexibility to shift output based on prices or seasonal demand, they are ultimately constrained by both chemistry and hardware. A refinery cannot simply decide one morning to turn an entire barrel of crude into jet fuel just because jet prices spiked overnight. Crude oil itself is not a single homogenous substance. Every barrel contains a different mix of molecules, and those differences largely determine what product a refinery can produce from it. Light crude flows more freely and contains a higher share of smaller hydrocarbon molecules, naturally yielding more gasoline and naphtha. Heavy crude is thick and dense, like molasses, and is packed with large, more complex molecules, tending to yield more diesel, fuel oil and residual products. At its core, refining is a mass-balance system: you cannot get out more than you put in. Refining is therefore fundamentally a zero-sum game. While they might not reveal a loss of confidence in the Fed’s ability to achieve its objective over longer time horizons, these measures can be critical for keeping inflation elevated for longer than the Fed is comfortable with. Recent analysis from the SF Fed (see here) shows that business inflation expectations, as captured by the CFO survey, have reliably predicted year-ahead inflation in recent decades. This measure of inflation expectations, which was set in Q4 2025, is consistent with some acceleration in inflation this year. In addition, prior work from the SF Fed has shown that short -run consumer inflation expectations ar e a more important determinant of wage growth (see here). As such, the surge in some of these measures should not be completely ignored , as they could lead to more persistent inflation pressures in the near term even if the Fed’s long-run credibility is not questioned. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Aluminium could also see further support, in LME prices or regional premiums, if we see further curtailments in the Middle East if the Strait of Hormuz is closed for longer, bringing shortages of raw materials to smelters that are still running. A meaningful drawdown in the remaining LME inventories, a limiting buffer in the market, could also push prices sharply higher. So far, end-user destocking has moderated the impact of the supply losses, and it is hard to predict how long this can continue, but it likely can't continue indefinitely, even if the backwardation persists. This could bring upside to both the LME price and regional premiums. Bear case: For now, we give higher probability to our bull case than our bear case. Our bear case sees aluminium falling to ~$2,500/t, which could come through on a more prolonged conflict, where aluminium's long positioning would likely work against it if demand destruction concerns came more into focus. A pick-up in exports from China could also help rebalance ex-China markets, but would likely also help to draw down China inventories.

records.text: 7 May 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 The Commission does not precisely quantify what constitutes a "severe economic downturn" for activating the GEC. However, we can look at the Vade Mecum guide to the Stability and Growth Pact (which outlined pre- reform rules) and past shocks offer some guidance. The Vade Mecum reports the necessary fiscal adjustments linked to cyclical conditions: if (annual) real GDP growth is negative or the output gap fell below -4%, the usual fiscal tightening in not required. Moreover, in March 2020, when the GEC was activated for the COVID-19 shock, the EC was expecting real GDP to contract by around 1%. While a marginal contraction might not suffice, the threshold for GEC activation could potentially be an outright decline in real GDP of at least 1%. n #2. National Escape Clause (NEC): A GEC is not the only mechanism for deviating from the EU's numerical fiscal rules. The alternative is the National Escape Clause (NEC). This can be activated by the Council upon request from a member state and a recommendation from the Commission. It would suspend fiscal rules solely for the requesting member state, provided that exceptional circumstances beyond its control have a major impact on its public finances. To sum up, the key distinction between the two escape clauses lies in their triggers. The GEC is activated by a severe downturn resulting from a common shock affecting all member states. records.text: Metal Matters 08 May 2026 Citi Research 6 Shift to a “just-in-case” world would require higher prices to meet the demand to build inventory As global concerns around the security of physical metal supply rise with growing trade and geopolitical friction, governments and private supply chains become more willing to hold higher levels of metals inventory as a buffer. This reflects a broader shift from optimizing purely for efficiency and “just‑in‑time” delivery toward resilience and a “just‑in‑case” approach. This has the potential structural requirement to build and maintain larger copper inventories and a surplus driven by deliberate stock‑building can coexist with, and even require, relatively high prices. This dynamic fits into the broader investor theme of building hard-asset exposure. As supply security becomes a priority, copper increasingly functions not just as an industrial input but also as a strategic asset. Producers, consumers, and governments alike have a greater incentive to secure material in advance, hedge raw‑material exposure, and reduce reliance on fragile supply chains. T o enable this, prices need to be high enough to incentivise additional supply, particularly from higher‑cost sources such as scrap and marginal mining capacity, beyond current demand. Holding copper inventory is not without cost, and higher interest rates can as a constraint by increasing financing costs. Given the volatility in recent LFS prints, and the survey’s sizeable standard error of roughly 32k, it remains difficult to extrapolate a materially weaker trend from a single monthly release. Instead, the data continue to support the view of an orderly slowing in labor market conditions rather than an abrupt downturn. The April employment report pointed to continued softness in labor market conditions following a brief stabilization in March, with total employment declining 17.7k and cumulative job losses now exceeding 110k over the first four months of 2026. While the report was soft at the margin, the signal remains somewhat ambiguous given the continued volatility in the LFS and the relatively small magnitude of the monthly decline relative to historical standard errors. More broadly, short-term employment trends continue to run below longer-term averages, consistent with a gradual slowing in labor demand rather than a sharp deterioration. Importantly, SEPH data, which we continue to view as the medium-term anchor for labor market conditions, deteriorated materially in February, falling to its weakest level in over two years. For now, we view both the payroll and household surveys as increasingly consistent directionally, pointing toward an orderly slowing in labor demand rather than a collapse in employment conditions. records.text: Because some parts of the breakeven accounting calculation are unclear—the pace of net immigration, the extent to which immigrant workers are captured by official statistics, and the path of the participation rate—we also consider a backward-looking approach that asks how many jobs would have been needed to stabilize the unemployment rate over the prior year. Specifically, we calculate backward-looking breakeven estimates as the average monthly increase in payroll or household employment over the prior 12 months plus the additional jobs that would have been needed to keep the unemployment rate stable (Exhibit 4). The implicit assumption in this approach is that labor force growth, the change in the participation rate, and any change in the gap between the payrolls and household measures of employment will be similar in the year ahead to last year’s trends. Because these factors can be volatile, backward-looking breakeven estimates—especially those based on household employment or shorter lookback horizons—can be very volatile, though the 12-month payrolls-based version is more stable and currently stands at about 30k per month. The note is organized into three sections: ▪ A model-based framework – page 2 ▪ An assessment of credibility costs – page 3 ▪ Empirical evidence on upside risks to inflation expectations – page 4 KEY MESSAGES Our model-based analysis suggests that the surprise hold from the Colombian central bank at the April meeting may have avoided a worse outcome relative to a 50bp hike, but the decision has likely left the policy rate further below the level implied by fundamentals. Past episodes and empirical studies show that one- year inflation expectations can rise more than 1pp when the market senses political interference in monetary policy decisions. We see risks to the terminal policy rate as skewed to the upside, driven by potential credibility costs and the effects of delayed tightening that could require an effort to re-anchor expectations. records.text: Our analysis reveals seasonal patterns in all Asian currencies around most key dividend payment periods (Figures 4 and 5). The patterns we observe have occurred about 67% of the time on average, in the past 15 years. You can see more on our methodology in Seasonality roadmap 2026 update, dated 30 January. However, while dividend payments can be meaningful, there are many reasons they may not generate an FX impact. For example, foreign ownership of local stocks may be low, companies/foreign shareholders may opt to pay/receive dividends in foreign currency (particularly if earnings are in FX), and the dividend flow may be spread out (making the relative impact small compared to the depth of the FX market). It may also be the case that foreign investors reinvest their dividends, or pre-hedge the FX risk associated to dividend earnings, and of course, other market events or dynamics can always be a greater focus. We think such factors may explain weaker or less-consistent patterns around the FX in some dividend periods. In particular, for the INR, IDR, PHP and VND, we note that total dividend payments in these regions are relatively small as a percentage of GDP and that the payments are more spread out. This contrasts with the period after Liberation Day, when investors were leaving the US to find more diversified investments. Now, the US seems better protected, experiencing less hardship in terms of interest rates. As a net energy exporter, the US is in a stronger position, whereas the UK, Eurozone, and Japan rely heavily on energy imports. Swapping EURNOK for USDNOK We decide to take profit on our short EURNOK position and substitute with a short USDNOK trade. Dollar flows are now the lowest they have been since December 2020 compelling us to add further short exposure to the dollar. Furthermore, this trade keeps us exposed to energy prices which will likely stay elevated in the near term. Oil and gas make up half of Norway’s exports, boosting its terms of trade. Additionally, NOK is one of the G10’s highest yielding currencies. Apr26 has seen an even more outsized increase, coinciding with a re-pricing of US rates post hawkish Fed, leading to questions about MAS’ policy bias on SGD rates. records.text: ing up over the past few years until recently, leading to slower property price appreciation. One of the key proposals from the New York governor is the construction of 200k rent-stabilized units. If it becomes a reality (even in a reduced capacity), it could have a material effect on long- term rent growth and vacancy levels, although a formal plan is not yet in place. For context, approximately 30k units have been delivered annually over the past three years; an addition of even 10k units per year would lead to higher vacancies and low rent growth. If construction focuses on the stabilized segment, it would also lead to a reduction in the supply of non- stabilized apartments, which could pose a significant risk to long-term NOI growth. The proposed pied-à-terre tax is more likely to materialize in the near term, given the lower hurdle for implementation, though it also must work through some operational challenges. This proposal introduces an annual surcharge on NYC second homes valued at $5mn or more, targeting non-resident owners. We would not expect the implementation of this tax to have material effect on the rental market, although it might free up some inventory at the top end. For the broader NYC economy, we believe there is too great a business reason to be based in the city, so the policy would be unlikely to cause a significant exodus. 8 May 2026 57 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Escalation aversion, for now

records.text: 8 May 2026 Fixed Income Blog Page 8 Deutsche Bank AG Twin Deficit Model Framework: We use the budget deficit and the current account deficit to construct the twin deficit (TD), equally weighted. Both are from the IMF's WEO. Our twin deficit score TDS(t) is a weighted average of recent years' TD, i.e., TD(t), TD(t-1), …, TD(t-5), assigning a larger weight to the most recent print. We also incorporate the cumulative sum of TD of previous years. That allows to capture both the flow and stock characteristics of this variable. We then run daily regressions of each year's TDS vs 10y EGB spreads to Bund. The regression excludes Italy, Portugal and Ireland. These daily regressions generate time series of the slope (proxy for market price of risk), the constant, and the residuals of each country's spread. records.text: circumstances necessitating investment in strategic autonomy, including defense. This can be viewed as an external shock beyond member states' control. Applying the Precedent to the Energy Shock: The precedent set by the defense spending NEC could clearly be extended to the current energy shock. The longer the shock persists, the greater the pressure on member states to shield households and firms. While the initial fiscal easing, worth 0.3% of GDP (annualised), was largely financed through budget savings, any additional spending would necessitate deficit financing, potentially leading to violations of fiscal rules. The difference with respect to the defence NEC is that the average member state is far away from satisfying the 2035 goal of raising core defence spending to 3.5% of GDP (5% of GDP including defence adjacent spending like infrastructure). Defence spending needs to rise a lot, both gradually and sustainably. The energy shock, on the other hand, will hopefully be a transitory shock - although depending on how transitory it is, it could still result in recession. On the other hand, a large and sustained fiscal cost could come from investing in strategic energy autonomy. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 08 May 2026 10:35:54 ET │ 12 pages Metal Matters We explore copper’s structural resilience to a cyclical growth shock while maintaining our near-term $13k/t target CITI'S TAKE We see resilience in copper's physical market in a bear case of prolonged Strait closure and a severe energy price shock given structural energy transition demand, military demand, and supply headwinds. Structural energy transition and AI demand now account for ~18% of consumption and can cushion cyclical demand headwinds. Supply-side impacts, particularly from scrap, in response to higher energy prices, also offers an offset. Geopolitical escalation in a growth-shock scenario could also boost military copper demand and underpin a "just-in-case" inventory shift to support higher medium-term copper prices. However, risk sentiment remains exposed to growth fears from the ongoing Hormuz closure in the coming weeks, and we maintain our near-term $13k/t copper price target. Copper looks supported near-term around $13k/t. We are cautious on pricing near term as our base case is continued Strait closure until end-May (See here) and risk- off on any US-Iran re-escalation could easily see prices ease lower. Even with a sharper risk sell-off we expect physical dip-buying to keep prices supported above $12k/t through 2Q’26. As noted above, RRF loans and their interest costs are repaid by the borrowing EU member states. At the time of writing, €157.6bn, or 73%, of the €216.7bn requested RRF loans have been disbursed, leaving €59.2bn of the RRF loan capacity (Figure 14). However, the RRF loan agreements offer much more lenient repayment requirements. First, each RRF loan disbursement will have a maturity of 30 years from the date of disbursement. Second, the loan agreements provide a 10y grace period on principal repayments and the only requirement is that the weighted average maturity of the RRF loan disbursements (for each country) is 20 years (see RRF Loan Agreement for Greece as an example). Based on this and the currently disbursed RRF loans, and assuming the remaining €59bn of RRF loans will be disbursed, the annual RRF loan principal repayments would be notably lower than RRF grant repayments (even under EC’s backloaded repayment schedule) staying below €10bn until 2036 (Figure 15). 0 5 10 15 20 25 28 30 32 34 36

We see periodic spikes in periods of solid labor markets, for example in the late 1980s and again in the late 1990s and again during the pandemic. This activity is a lot less than pre-1981. Of course, even so, among unionized workers in the economy, the willingness to strike for periods of time is infrequent, and only perks up when labor market alternatives are relatively healthy. In a way, that is likely a sign of bargaining power. When labor is becoming more expensive and more scarce, workers are willing to negotiate more forcefully for higher wages. In 2025, the activity languished near series lows. Not a strong sign of those workers' perceptions of their bargaining power and ability to win higher wages in negotiation. In two papers in the early 1970s, the first an analysis of quit rates in manufacturing, and the second an analysis of quit rates in the context of a more fully fleshed out model, John Pencavel placed the quit rate in the middle of a wage-bargaining model noting how higher wages tended to lower quit rates. (6) . In that context, the quit rate was a sign of the bargaining power of the worker, and the firm needed to reduce quits to earn returns from on-the-job training, for example. Our base case is headwinds from US tariff and inventory dynamics see copper prices moderate to $12k/t by 4Q’26 while our bull case sees an improvement in growth expectations as Hormuz reopens, restocking, or renewed momentum in energy-transition demand (as a structural reaction to the Hormuz crisis even once reopened) sees prices averaging $15k/t by year-end. Already-robust energy transition copper demand can partly offset the cyclical copper demand impact of an energy price shock by driving incremental electric vehicle, renewables and power grid-demand. Assuming energy transition demand growth stays intact or strengthens, global copper demand could avoid contraction even with a 3% hit to annual cyclical copper demand, a level almost equivalent to major historical annual refined copper demand shocks of -3% to -5%. China's copper consumption looks more resilient given higher energy transition exposure, while ex-China consumption is most cyclically exposed. Rising and more equipment‑intensive military spending can also underpin copper demand resilience and offer upside in response to further geopolitical escalation. Global defence budgets are set to grow modestly, but there is scope for sharp increases under escalation scenarios. Increasing copper intensity from modern, equipment‑heavy warfare could also see military‑related copper consumption outpace real‑terms spending

records.text: 12 US Economic Viewpoint | 07 May 2026 More recently, fiscal policy will likely exacerbate K-shaped spending dynamics in coming months. The passage of the OBBBA last year relied heavily on deductions and tax-base adjustments, making its benefits more valuable for households with higher taxable income and marginal tax rates. We have estimated that the bill is most beneficial for middle- and higher-income households. The bottom two income quintiles will likely see only modest gains. That’s because most of the stimulus provisions are deductions, which lower tax bills more for households that have a higher marginal tax rate. Estimates from the Yale Budget Lab suggest that the fourth income quintile (roughly $75k–$140k) will receive the largest refund boost relative to income, followed by the third ($45k–$75k) and top (> $140k) quintiles. In the last couple of months, we have been seeing that OBBBA-related tax refunds during the tax season have been running above last year’s level, albeit slightly lesser than initial expectations (Exhibit 23Exhibit 23). But the largest incremental boost has likely been accruing to higher-income households, as expected. Indeed, this is evident in BAC data, which show that year-to-date 2026 tax refund growth has been stronger for higher-income households than for lower-income households, reversing last year’s pattern (Exhibit 24). Oil prices absorb enormous amounts of information with remarkable speed. That raises an important question: how should we interpret Brent averaging only about $100 in the two months since the war began despite the largest supply disruption on record? Rather than signaling complacency, the market may be acknowledging a harsher reality: a shock of this magnitude cannot be absorbed through the crude market alone. There is simply not enough elasticity on the crude side of the system. Instead, the adjustment is increasingly being pushed down the barrel—out of crude and into refined products. Crude shortages have already forced refiners across Asia and Europe to cut runs by 2.1 mbd in March and 3.8 mbd in April. At the same time, the market has also lost an estimated 4.7 mbd of refined product exports from the Middle East itself.
