There is a growing group of investors sympathetic to the view that measurable gains of AI could appear in a structural way sooner rather than later across the corporate universe and labour markets, but policymakers like ECB GC member Schnabel (2026) have also emphasized that AI is more likely to be inflationary than disinflationary in the short run, given large investments needs in energy-intensive data centres and risks of new bottlenecks in specialised chips and skilled labour. Chad Jones (2026) also points out that new technologies tend to diffuse gradually and that the weakest links tend to constrain increases in production (in line with a "business as usual scenario"). Furthermore, professor Jones also warns that countries may be underinvesting in AI safety spending, and he estimates that the willingness to pay for safer AI could be as high as 100% of GDP in the US. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 08 May 2026 17:11:28 ET │ 14 pages Canada Economics Weekly Market pricing disconnected from data CITI'S TAKE This week’s data did little to change our view that the Canadian economy warrants rate cuts much more than rate hikes, even with markets continuing to price ~40bp worth of hikes this year. The unemployment rate rose to 6.9% in April, close to recent highs, and real trade data reaffirm that falling exports and rising imports will weigh substantially on Q1 GDP . Still, details of Q1 domestic demand could look stronger, and data over the next few months are unlikely to substantially shift market pricing or BoC guidance. But we continue to think softer growth and at-or-below target inflation will have BoC officials cutting rates again later this year. In 2021, markets found their footing after Velarde was confirmed to remain at the BCRP, which calmed investors by reinforcing the perception of central bank inde- pendence. This time around, Velarde’s expressed preference not to pursue a fifth term (his mandate ends in July 2026) adds another layer of uncertainty to the mix. In any case, although the Central Bank has sufficient reserves to step in and contain excessive volatility in the FX market, we do not think they would pursue a full reversal of any depreciation trend justified by fundamental changes in economic policy in the country. In the 2021 election, for example, although the central bank did not announce a formal intervention mecha- nism in the FX market, it sold ~USD 11bn in the spot from March 2021 to March 2022, a sizeable amount that, neverthe- less, did not prevent the depreciation trend. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. Long-end Japanese yields have continued to climb this year, with 10y yields at levels last sustained in the 1990s. LLC Global Markets Daily: A More Durable Risk Premium in JGBs 8 May 2026 | 7:59AM EDT We are raising our long-end JGB forecasts to reflect a more durable risk premium n across the curve. We now see 10y JGBs at 2.50% at end-2026 and 2.25% at end-2027, versus 2% previously across both years. Evidence from G4 curves since the start of the oil shock suggests that a more n front-footed hawkish central bank reaction can limit the rise in long-end risk premia. For Japan, the market is pricing a terminal rate consistent with our economists’ 1.5% baseline, but risk premium has built further out the curve, in contrast to the clearer flattening across the US, UK, and Europe. Unlike last year, when the cheapness along the JGB curve was most pronounced n at the very long-end, underperformance versus the macro backdrop has migrated in towards the belly of the curve. Idiosyncratic supply and demand factors remain an episodic source of long-end volatility, but the broader year-to-date trend in yields and the curve appears to reflect macro dynamics related to domestic inflation and fiscal risks, alongside higher yields globally. Without a more proactive approach from the BoJ or a reduction in inflation n uncertainty, we think that higher yields can persist, with the belly of the curve the likely pressure release valve to any further rise in inflation or fiscal worries. records.text: Marija Veitmane 07 May 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Earnings week 4 : Something is rotten in the state of European profitability A narrative is building that European equities stand to benefit the most from a potential US–Iran peace settlement. After all, the region has been seen as the key loser from the conflict, with higher energy costs forcing a more hawkish ECB stance and undermining an already fragile recovery. In that sense, unwinding the “war discount” could support European equities, while removing the safe-haven bid for the US. We strongly disagree. The core issue for Europe remains weak earnings. While a resolution would help, it is unlikely to materially close the earnings gap with the US. We therefore maintain a clear preference for US equities; hence we maintain our strong preference for US over Europe. The latest earnings season illustrates the problem. Expectations were already low—roughly half those of the US—yet only a modest share of companies beat, and by a small margin (Figure 1). Guidance has also disappointed, limiting any positive market reaction (Figure 2). At the sector level, Industrials—both a heavy index weight and a key earnings driver—had a particularly weak quarter. Earnings surprises were among the lowest, with even high-profile names such as Rheinmetall struggling to meet expectations. However, as argued a month ago, if we assume away the risks to employment from AI and the Iran war, the data are not consistent with Fed cuts. Indeed, even under that scenario, core inflation would remain comfortably above 2% for the next 18 months. Lending standards remain consistent with growth around potential, and financial conditions do not indicate that monetary policy is too tight. Finally, labour market data continue to point to a stabilisation. This is in line with both our structural and cyclical views. From a structural perspective, we argued that the neutral rate is likely to be closer to 4% than 3% as the imbalances in the supply/demand of savings unwind. From a cy clical perspective, the shift in the policy mix from tight monetary and fiscal in 2025 to neutral monetary and easy fiscal in 2026 should be reflected in a stabilisation of the labour market. records.text: 2 US Watch | 08 May 2026 Market response: Rates and FX Rates: solid but not game changing US rates declined modestly following the April employment report, though moves were small. US rates declined due to mixed messages in the labor report. Specifically, the establishment survey beat expectations but the household survey reflected cooler labor market (U3 higher on unrounded basis, wages soft). Overall the US rates market did little to re-price expectations for the Fed. The market continues to expect a Fed hold over the next several meetings with some small risk of rate hikes (~33% odds of 1 25bp hike over next 1Y). On net, the print did little to change our core rate views. We continue to like being tactically paid the US rate front end with an overall economy & labor market that has demonstrated strong resilience since the start of the commodity shock. We will adjust views if there are broader signs of economic cooling over time. FX: not exciting enough for the USD bulls The FX market’s reaction to today’s decent US labor report was relatively modest. Despite the upside surprise in headline NFP, the USD is roughly 0.1%-0.2% lower vs. most G10 currencies, with broader directional moves more driven by the household survey results. records.text: he employment fell by 0.1pp to 60.6% (Exhibit 3). Jobs losses centered on the goods sector Job destruction was centered in the goods producing sector (-26.8k) were all subsectors posted a loss, with construction (-15.7k), and natural resources (-5.5k) leading the way (Exhibit 5). Manufacturing shed jobs again, with an ytd loss of -35.7k (Exhibit 6). This was slightly offset by the services sector (+9.1k), on the back of business, building & other support services (+21.5k). However, employment fell in information, culture & recreation (-24.8k), and ‘other’ services (-12.7k), with trade (-8.3k) also posting losses. Trade and transport keep shrinking, likely on heightened USMCA-related uncertainty. Unemployment rate rises to 6.9% The unemployment rate rose 0.2pp to 6.9% (E. 6.7%, BofA 6.8%) (Exhibit 4), as the participation rate rose due to more people searching for work. Specifically, the participation rate went up by 0.1pp to 65.0% in April, after remaining unchanged in March. Hourly wage growth decelerated to 4.5% yoy from 4.7% in March (Exhibit 8). Overall, the rise in unemployment underscores continued weakness in the Canadian economy, which is likely to further deteriorate the ongoing oil price shock. BoC: We continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold We continue to expect the BoC to hold the policy rate at 2.25% through year end (see our BoC Canada Watch). The CIT ruling was a split decision, with two Democratic-appointed judges granting summary judgment against the administration’s position and one Republican-appointed judge dissenting, favoring a full review of the case instead. This is in contrast to the CIT’s earlier ruling last year, in which a panel of one Democratic- and two Republican-appointed judges unanimously granted summary judgment against the IEEPA tariffs. 2. The CIT ruling gives the administration 5 days to rescind the tariffs, and requires that importers be paid refunds plus interest. We expect the administration to immediately appeal the ruling to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC), as it did following the CIT’s IEEPA ruling. In that instance, the CAFC stayed the CIT ruling within a day, leaving the tariffs in effect, and then took 3 months to rule on the case. That ruling was then appealed to SCOTUS, which took another 6 months to rule. As the Sec. 122 tariffs expire July 24 and cannot be extended without an act of Congress, an eventual SCOTUS ruling against these tariffs looks unlikely to come before expiration. records.text: fuel‑pricing mechanisms, not exposure to global oil markets, in our view. We study the fuel markets across the region and classify them into three broad categories, including regulated markets (Malaysia, Indonesia), quasi- regulated markets (Thailand, Vietnam, India, Japan, China, Taiwan, Korea) and liberalized markets (Philippines, Singapore). Empirical evidence suggested liberalized markets show the clearest and fastest pass‑through, while regulated markets would generally witness the least. Those with thin policy buffers tend to prioritize inflation Since the outbreak of the Middle East tensions, policymakers’ primary focus has shifted to price stability by managing the initial supply shock, and containing any potential second-round effects. In our view, an economy with 1) a more liberalized fuel market, 2) higher energy import dependence, and 3) less fiscal buffer to provide cost-of-living relief measures tend to have stronger tightening bias to anchor inflation expectation. Philippines is the best example under our case study. FX and growth concerns complicate CB decisions Nonetheless, the inflation impact from the energy shock is not the only policy concern for monetary authorities. We believe regional central banks’ decisions can be further complicated by other factors, such as the output gap and FX pressure, leading to divergent monetary policy paths ahead. Accordingly, we compare the Dallas Fed to two symmetric trimmed means (Exhibit 1). The first trims 8% off the top and bottom, mirroring the Cleveland Fed’s trimmed-mean CPI calculation. The second trims 24% off both sides. So it only differs from the Dallas Fed measure in one way: it trims 7% less off the top of the distribution. In March, the Dallas Fed measure stood at 2.4%, continuing its recent downtrend. Meanwhile, our 8% symmetric trim has been rising recently and stood at 2.9% in March. The 24% symmetric trim has been cooling but remains elevated at 2.7%. Each of these signals could have different implications for monetary policy. For reference, core PCE inflation was 3.2% y/y. Another drawback of the trimmed measure is that it tends to lag core inflation around turning points. We saw this in 2008 and 2009, when core cooled sharply, and in 2021- 2022, when core surged. This means that a focus on the trimmed mean could leave the Fed behind the curve. … And switching focus now creates credibility issues In addition to these drawbacks, the clearest argument for the Fed to continue to emphasize the traditional core is credibility. records.text: US Economics 08 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – Nonfarm payroll employment rose by 115k jobs in April, stronger than consensus expectations at 65k and our forecast for a 15k decline. Private industry employment rose by 123k. Manufacturing employment fell by 2k jobs while construction added 9k. Services employment was more broad-based, with strength in trade/transportation (+60k), health care and social assistance (+54k), and leisure/hospitality (+14k). Average hourly earnings rose a modest 0.2% and 3.6%YoY, up from a downwardly revised 3.4%YoY in March. The unemployment rate rose from 4.26% to 4.34%, remaining at 4.3% on a rounded basis. This was despite another decline in the labor force participation rate from 61.9% to 61.8%. The unemployment rate would have increased to 4.42% if the participation rate had remained unchanged. Citi’s view – Stronger payroll employment for the second month in a row in April has broken a pattern of very volatile job growth month-to-month, oscillating between positive and negative for close to a year. Over the last 6 months, payroll job growth has picked up, averaging around 55k. The unemployment rate also remained within its recent range at 4.3%, with very little in April data to change Fed officials’ recent assessment that the labor market is stabilizing. Accordingly, Japanese authorities do not conduct intervention with the aim of reversing the yen’s trend determined by fundamentals, and all interventions are posited to be smoothing operations. The government does not want USD/JPY to continue rising above 160, while it also likely wants to avoid materially reducing FX reserves. Because the outstanding amount of the FX reserve is perceived as reflect- ing Japan’s capacity for yen-buying intervention, a sharp fall could be seen as reduced intervention capacity and raise the risk of inviting speculative attacks. Therefore, if the structural depreciation pressure on the yen persists, the MoF will likely be forced at some point to give up defending 160 yen. The February improvement may have been helped by more favorable weather conditions, and the January level was an unusually low outlier, with some level correction to be expected. Mortgage rates also fell to near 6% in February before backing up to their January levels in March. All told, the March level of sales landed close to our 682K expectations. The NHS data are often heavily revised, and revisions across November through January revised up a cumulative 4K. Inventories remain elevated, but two months of better weather conditions shaved off some inventory after subdued sales in January. Months' supply at the current sales pace fell 0.7 to 9.1 months in February and then fell 0.6 to 8.5 months in March, back toward the recent range. The openings rate is generally consistent with a pre-pandemic Beveridge Curve relationship. Quits still low, suggesting subdued worker confidence. Sales up on net in February and March after an unusually low January.

The gap between US monetary policy and that of other G7 nations becomes apparent when comparing sovereign yield curves, as the current conflict has intensified strain on international bond markets far more than on those in the US (chart overleaf). As a result, other countries are under greater pressure to respond, which likely contributed to reports of intervention by Japanese officials last week in the JPY. Overall, we maintain our short position on the US dollar against the NZD and have elected to further increase our dollar short exposure by substituting our EURNOK short with a USDNOK short position (2nd chart overleaf). At the same time, it seems inevitable that the ECB will respond with a hike over the medium term (another reason why we took profit on EURNOK), and it's likely the BoE will need to take action too, which could put extra strain on an economy already facing challenges. For this reason, we continue holding a two-unit short position in GBP against both JPY and NZD. Finally, we maintain our long position in CADCHF to balance our commodity exposure, since Canada is also experiencing significant benefits from an improved terms of trade. records.text: 8 May 2026 US Economic Perspectives Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 1. Underlying/trend inflation remains near 3% There is a prevailing wisdom that underlying or trend inflation has continued to make progress towards the Fed’s 2% inflation objective. Barring one or two exceptions, this view is inconsistent with a holistic account of measures of trend inflation. Among popular measures of PCE trend inflation, core (3.2%), NY Fed’s multivariate inflation gauge (3.2%), and median (2.8%) remain centered around 3% -- a full percentage point above target. Our dashboard of trend measures of inflation shows that a more co mplete view of underlying inflation, based on the Fed staff’s own research (see here), supports the conclusion that trend inflation has remained in a tight range 75 -100bps above the Fed’s target for the past two years. The lone outlier to this conclusion is trimmed mean PCE. While trimmed mean can be a preferred gauge of underlying inflation during periods of low and stable inflation, recent research from the Dallas Fed (see here), who construct and publishes the official trimmed mean PCE gauge, shows that this metric is biased lower when the skew of the price distribution is positive, as is currently the case. Housing starts have been elevated in Canada in recent years, largely driven by the multifamily sector Canadian home builders have responded to the persistent housing shortage as well as government policies/incentives for home building in recent years. Canadian housing starts over the past six months have averaged 24% higher than the 2019 average vs. the US being just 8% higher. Housing starts in Canada have remained at elevated levels since the onset of the pandemic while they have declined in the US after a short-lived spike in 2021-22 (Exhibit 4). records.text: sufficient balances to cover all gross maturing debt as well as net fiscal outflows. Over the past year, that policy has at times implied TGA balances in excess of $1tn. Treasury primarily builds the TGA through bill issuance, but because bill auction sizes are adjusted only gradually, issuance must often occur well in advance of anticipated cash needs. This can result in periods when TGA balances temporarily exceed the minimum implied by the cash management policy, leaving Treasury with excess cash. TBAC was therefore asked to explore whether this excess cash could be placed into the repo market, reflecting Treasury’s broader effort to manage the TGA more efficiently given its larger structural size. The growing focus on TGA management also reflects its role on the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet. Alongside currency in circulation and reserve balances, the TGA is one of the Fed’s largest liabilities. As policymakers and market participants continue to debate the appropriate size of the Fed’s balance sheet , improved TGA management is increasingly viewed as a potential avenue through which the Fed could operate with a smaller balance sheet, all else equal. Large and rapid swings in the TGA—particularly around tax payment dates—also introduce volatility into reserve balances, since increases in the TGA drain reserves from the banking system. records.text: US Rates Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 18 TBAC discussions – nothing too exciting Turning to the discussion points, Treasury reported that the “proposed changes to bank capital were expected to result in incremental additional demand for Treasury securities from depository institutions as well as unlock balance sheet space that would most likely be deployed to repo.” We summarized the current proposals in US Rates Weekly: Rate pause pro tem, and the next milestone for the proposal is the end of the comment period which ends on June 18th. Turning to the first charge, TBAC, which is a collection of buy-side and sell-side market participants, discussed the expansion of central clearing in the Treasury securities market. The Committee highlighted that inter-affiliate Treasury transactions and extraterritorial reach transactions between non-US participants remain as ongoing issues. The second charge was around Treasury investment in repo, specifically whether Treasury could invest “excess” TGA balance in the repo market. TBAC argued that the “definition of excess cash would govern how much cash is available to invest”; as a reminder, Treasury aims to hold one week’s worth of outflows on hand, and we do not think this target would change in the near term. Separately, the Committee also mentioned that the design choices of this mechanism would “influence how much volatility resides in the TGA and the repo investments.” T-bill auctions to grow in May, but expect June cuts On T-bil

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 08 May 2026 07:00:00 ET │ 13 pages The Speculative Grade Beat Rating Agencies: What AI Disruption? CITI'S TAKE Considering all the negative press credit has received since late 2025, rating actions are surprisingly constructive. Sentiment is weak in select pockets, but agencies are upgrading loans across the rating spectrum and the market’s largest sectors. We dive into the rating actions, looking for broader ramifications. Next, we revisit our AI Risk Score framework applied to software loans, finding it to be the clearest return differentiator within B1/B2 rated credits — and a meaningful early warning signal for near-term refinancing risk. Rating Agencies: What AI Disruption? — The divergence between market pricing and rating agency action is striking as the downgrade/upgrade ratio reaches its best level in years. We find both BBB/BB and single-B loans have improving downgrade/upgrade ratios, driven by upgrades. Improvement also spans the largest sectors. We discuss implications for rating-sensitive investors and BDCs. Market Responds: AI Risk Score Is a Return Differentiator — Within the B1/B2 cohort, AI Risk Score produced meaningful return differentiation — a finding made more compelling by the fact that these are relatively healthy speculative-grade credits. Higher-for-longer oil and rates = short consumer sectors: Resilient US macro conditions, flows, and a robust earnings season have lifted stock indices to record-high levels, despite oil and back-end rates also near YTD highs. That equity-beta lift has helped even those sectors more vulnerable to rising oil and rates – i.e. consumer staples and discretionary. Staples still lead SPX YTD (8% versus 6%), while discretionary have cut their underperformance, largely on the back of Amazon, so far in Q2. records.text: ural reforms to increase competitiveness are needed. Short-term, higher domestic demand could help. And indeed, consumption growth, supported by strong real wage gains, was one of the key growth drivers in the euro area in past years (1.5pp cumulatively in 2024 and 2025, i.e. 65% of EA growth). The energy shock directly affects that growth pillar, as higher inflation will reduce consumption growth, all else equal. This is the main reason we have lowered our growth forecast since the start of the Middle East conflict. The expected negative growth impact so far is limited and concentrated in 2026 - but it is increasing with the duration of the energy price shock and could become much larger (see here). A more subtle impact of the energy shock is that it takes away a potential driver of significant upside to growth, at least for some time: the elevated economic uncertainty is likely to be bad news for anyone who was banking on a boost to European growth from a fall in the savings rate. And this leads us to our topic of the day: the evolution of the euro area household savings rate. It currently stands at 14.4%, almost 2ppt above its pre-pandemic average. The savings rate increased strongly during the pandemic and then fell back to around 13% at the end of 2022. Since then, it has increased again and a key question for the euro area outlook has been whether that increase would reverse. Scorecard values are not directly comparable across markets or indicators, as each reflects the relative position of its own signal within its historical context and does not indicate the absolute strength or intensity of the view. Individual signals are mapped to the -5/+5 scorecard scale based on their percentile rank within their historical distribution using a starndard lookback period as in our GFIMs publications for fair value models and a 2Y lookback period for the other variables. records.text: M Idea 2 Slowing Down – Bottom Up Feedback Unlike many shocks and crises over the past two decades, Australia now faces a more direct impact. The energy price shock has proven more acute than for peers, and supply risks remain elevated as Middle East volumes stay curtailed. A return of inflation pressures is driving policy responses that firmly target housing and consumption to slow these segments as a mitigation of current risks. This links to the fact that much of the investment and capex pipeline reflects structural drivers and shows less sensitivity to interest rates. As a result, the coming slowdown requires consumers to spend less, house prices to adjust lower, and labor markets to loosen. Conference season now tests this macro view through company updates as trading statements begin to emerge. We review key sectors to assess cost pressures, how companies are implementing mitigation strategies, and what, if anything, they are signalling on the outlook for demand. Cost Pressures Evident Company commentary increasingly suggests that the energy shock is now showing up across cost bases. Higher fuel prices are feeding into freight, logistics, construction, claims, livestock, and a widening range of input costs, with more companies flagging second‑round impacts across maintenance and technology as well. records.text: scal consolidation to stall; recovery funds increasingly at risk A new government led by another PNL PM would likely ease near‑term investor concerns around political instability, particularly as no major fiscal slippage is expected in 2026. However, we are sceptical about Romania’s ability to deliver further structural reforms and sustain fiscal consolidation over the medium term. Risks around the absorption of EU recovery funds are also rising meaningfully. EUR 10bn gross (EUR 7.7bn net) in RRF financing is scheduled for 3Q–4Q 2026 (Exhibit 14). According to outgoing PM Bolojan, up to EUR 7.3bn (gross) could be forfeited if outstanding legislation is not completed on time (Exhibit 15). This would represent a material risk to growth, policy credibility, and market sentiment. Downgrade risks rising, but still require concrete triggers The negative outlook on the credit is likely to persist. However, clearer evidence of fiscal slippage and/or market pressure would be required for a tangible increase in downgrade risk to sub‑IG. At this stage, we maintain our forecast for the budget deficit at around 6.5% of GDP in 2026 versus the official target of 6.2%, with the deficit easing to around 6% in 2027. That said, greater PSD influence within the next government would clearly undermine the already challenging path towards a 3% of GDP deficit over the longer term.

We stick with our (-12bp, -8bp) range and would prefer fading moves when spreads are at the top end of that range. With Schatz spreads around ~ -10bp, we stay neutral. Bund: swapped & govie issuance are the swing factors. For Bund spreads, Germany’s funding considerations and swapped issuance remain the most relevant short-term drivers. On funding, we do not expect a material narrowing from any sharp pickup in net issuance: Euro area governments have so far adopted only modest fiscal measures in response to the energy shock, and the broader fiscal response should remain limited unless the situation becomes substantially worse (see Euro Cash). records.text: Short-End Notes 08 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Repo markets this week continued to show signs that liquidity in the system is plentiful. Yesterday SOFR fixed 5bp below IORB, the lowest level since early April and Aug-25 before then (see Figure 1). Notably, we also saw effective FF tick one bp lower yesterday. We think this move could be a one-off event, driven by a combination of higher FF volume and a relatively lower TGCR rate. On the volume side, we had argued before that FF volumes were likely to pick up following the April 15 Tax Day, and, as we show Figure 2, FF volume is back to the levels from last summer. It is possible that the deluge of liquidity via the Fed’s Reserve Management Purchases has limited demand for FHLB advances, and thus there is an overallocation to Fed funds by the FHLBs. That, combined with TGCR below EFFR likely put downward pressure on EFFR. For now, we don’t expect to see EFFR continuing to move lower and instead think it’s possible that this move lower is undone in the near term. We think May SOFR/FF is somewhat insulated from this move in EFFR. Or, in other words, EFFR will only keep going lower in the short-term if TGCR stays roughly under 3.6%; thus SOFR/FF probably realizes at higher levels if EFFR keeps falling. records.text: Buybacks We forecast S&P 500 gross buybacks will grow by +3% in 2026 and +5% in 2027. We model annual S&P 500 buyback growth as a function of earnings growth, valuation, policy uncertainty, and financial conditions. Historically, earnings growth has been the most important driver of buyback growth. However, rising equity valuations, higher policy uncertainty, and tighter borrowing conditions have contributed to relatively weak growth in buybacks in recent quarters. Data from the GS Buybacks Desk suggest volumes YTD are tracking at 1.1x the level of 2025 activity. Reduced buyback activity among the hyperscalers will weigh on aggregate S&P 500 buybacks. Hyperscaler capex has come at the expense of buybacks, which fell by 64% year/year during 1Q. The group now allocates 15% of total cash spending on buybacks compared with an average of 27% from 2017-2022. We expect hyperscaler buyback growth will likely stagnate through 2027. With all of cash flows from operations expected to be allocated towards capex, it leaves less room to return cash to shareholders without a sharp deceleration in capex growth, a drawdown of cash balances, or an increase in debt. Increased buybacks from Banks and the beneficiaries of AI capex, such as semis, should help offset some of those headwinds. records.text: Metal Matters 08 May 2026 Citi Research 3 Today copper looks more resilient to a cyclical growth shock comparable with prior major global downturn. Total copper demand could avoid contraction even with a 3% annual cyclical demand hit (almost equivalent to prior major growth shocks). Historically, major downturns such as the 1980s second oil shock and the Global Financial Crisis saw copper demand fall by roughly 3–5% on an annual basis (Fig.4). If we assumed a similar shock today was contained to cyclical copper demand segments and assumed structural growth across energy transition and AI demand remained intact, then a 5% contraction to cyclical demand segments would translate to a ‑1.7% annual refined copper consumption hit, while a 3% cyclical demand hit would imply broadly flat global demand. This illustrates how the growing structural demand share dampens risks to total aggregate physical demand for copper. Also important to note is traditional cyclical copper demand has already been relatively weak since 2022 in an environment of high interest rates and muted global manufacturing activity. That could also limit the scale of any further downside adjustment in the event of a growth shock versus past cycles which cyclical consumption from a stronger base. Figure 4. records.text: The AI boom is having a large impact both on corporate spending decisions and the way investors are reacting to those decisions. Investor appetite for companies investing for future growth is always conditional on the expected returns on those investments. Today, the returns of many ongoing investment initiatives will depend on the extent of value creation and disruption catalyzed by AI adoption. As a result, changes in the outlook for AI will also affect investor appetite for companies prioritizing growth investment spending. Recent weakness in corporate buyback growth should also support a continued scarcity premium for companies returning cash to shareholders. A portfolio of “Buyback Aristocrats” that have consistently repurchased stocks during the past decade has lagged the market during the last few months after outperforming earlier this year. The median Buyback Aristocrat trades at a 5% P/E premium to the equal-weight S&P 500. records.text: If the labor market does not weaken sufficiently this year, we would instead expect the FOMC to deliver two final cuts in 2027, when we expect core inflation to return to the 2% target. We have left our terminal rate forecast of 3-3.25% unchanged because FOMC participants’ projections of the neutral rate have been fairly stable recently, and most still envision at least a couple more cuts eventually. But we do see a reasonable chance that if the economy holds up at the current funds rate all year, more FOMC participants could raise their estimates of neutral and conclude that further cuts are unnecessary. Exhibit 3 shows our updated Fed scenario analysis. We now put a 10% probability on modest rate hikes, a 25% probability on the FOMC leaving the funds rate unchanged indefinitely, a 40% probability on our baseline where the final two cuts now come in December and March, and a 25% probability (down from 30% previously) on a recession over the next year. Even after pushing back the cuts in our baseline, allowing for the possibility that the FOMC could stay on hold indefinitely, and nudging down our recession probability, our probability-weighted funds rate forecast remains meaningfully more dovish than market pricing, largely because we remain much more skeptical of rate hikes. records.text: , Barclays Research Despite material involvement in enabling DC build-out, utilities' funding needs for AI/data centers are an order of magnitude lower. AI/data centers are driving a substantial investment opportunity set for regulated utilities by way of new generation and grid infrastructure. The sector has identified well over a 250GW high probability large-load pipeline over the next 10 years. However, with incremental natural gas generation build costs of $2.5-3bn/GW and grid connection costs, at least initially, $0.25bn/GW, the annual investment growth opportunity is much lower than in Tech. Data center/AI-related investment of over $500bn for the sector over the next year 10 years compares with over $250bn of annual sector capex. Moreover, the sector has diversified sources of financing: currencies, convertibles, DOE loans, and securitization that have limited index-eligible IG funding increases to +$10bn y/y (we estimate $140bn this year). 8 May 2026 38 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Escalation aversion, for now

records.text: y’s visit (11-13 May) US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will pay a visit to Japan on 11-13 May, where he will meet in succession with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, and BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda. The focus will be America’s stance on forex given the rising market vigilance over potential market intervention by Japanese monetary authorities. Any remarks by Bessent aimed at curbing the yen’s depreciation could have a substantial impact on forex markets. Another key point will be whether the discussion touches upon Japanese monetary policy as a means of correcting the weakness in the nation’s currency. records.text: 2 US Economic Viewpoint | 07 May 2026 A resilient consumer, but with a narrow foundation US consumer spending has remained resilient in the last year despite a cooling labor market, a big tariff shock and elevated interest rates. However, this resilience has become increasingly concentrated among higher-income households. Lower-income spending is just treading water, resulting in “K-shaped” spending dynamics. K-shaped spending reinforced by a K-shaped economy Higher-income households have sustained consumption through stronger wealth effects from buoyant equities markets, stable housing costs, steadier labor market outcomes and greater insulation from higher interest rates, which has kept credit conditions healthier. Lower-income households, by contrast, have faced a combination of limited exposure to equity market gains, rising rents, slower job growth and elevated debt- servicing costs. In the coming months, two factors are likely to reinforce this divergence. First, higher- income spending should get a bigger boost from tax-related OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) stimulus. Second, the rise in energy prices due to the Iran war will almost certainly deliver an asymmetric shock to household purchasing power. Higher energy costs tend to function as a regressive tax, weighing more heavily on lower-income households that spend a larger share of their income on gasoline and other energy- intensive necessities. With China hitting its smelting capacity cap and tight power markets constraining supply elsewhere, this pushes the market into a 1.85 Mt deficit for 2026 on our estimates. Timespreads and regional premiums better reflect the tightness so far: With this deficit, many investors are asking why the LME 3m aluminium price is only up 12% since the start of the conflict. However, spot prices are up 14% as the forward curve has tightened, while regional premiums have rallied strongly – European duty-paid premium +55%, MJP (Japan) +72% and Midwest premium +9%. Demand destruction/deferral may also be holding prices/premiums back: Exhibit 2 shows the sharp shift in the forward curve, with Dec'26 aluminium now trading $160/t below spot. While this can contribute to the 'roll yield' for financial participants, it makes holding excess inventory punitive for end users as the value of material erodes over time. Our economists are expecting 0.36% MoM seasonally adjusted core inflation (see US Economics - CPI Preview – April CPI strong on gas prices, shelter catch up). While that might seem like a big jump from the 0.2% MoM prints in February and March, part of it is because it includes two months of shelter inflation. Due to the lack of data during the government shutdown in October, the November inflation print only accounted for one month of shelter inflation (OER and Rent). The April data will now capture both the MoM shelter inflation in April and the missed month of shelter inflation in October. However, this should not be a surprise, and inflation markets are already pricing for this. We do not expect 1y inflation swap pricing to change significantly unless core inflation is higher than 0.4% in April. Services ex-shelter and core goods inflation will be the key. records.text: US Economics Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Data released this week did not cause us to significantly adjust our economic outlook. Payroll employment increased by 100k+ for two consecutive months for the first time since 2024. But we continue to see the labor market as stable, but fragile, with weak labor demand matched by equally weak labor supply. We see little evidence that the economy is “reaccelerating” but rather that it continues to expand at around a 2% real rate with about half of that growth due to AI-related investment. Headline job growth was stronger than expected at 115k in April, above consensus for 65k and our forecast for a 15k decline. But underlying details were softer than the headline beat. The unemployment rate moved higher from 4.26% to 4.34% despite a decline in labor force participation. Unemployment has been stable in a 4.3-4.5% range. But the pattern in the last two years is for a stable unemployment rate at the start of the year to give way to increasing unemployment over the summer months. A similar pattern this year could quickly raise dovish concerns about the strength of the labor market. Figure 1. Payroll job growth has been volatile over the last year Figure 2. records.text: Our 2026 baseline is somewhat higher than estimates recently published by Fed economists for two reasons. First, many of these Fed estimates have relied on a much lower net immigration estimate from Brookings, which assumes much larger voluntary outflows of unauthorized immigrants. We are skeptical that voluntary departures have risen as much as Brookings’ estimates suggest, but it is possible that some immigrants without work permits have shifted to parts of the economy less captured by official statistics. Using the Brookings immigration estimate would lower our estimate of the breakeven rate to about 40k per month currently and 30k by year-end. Second, some of these estimates appear to have assumed that the outsized declines in the participation rate over the past year—caused in part by the delayed incorporation of data from the 2020 Census in the annual adjustment to the household survey’s population controls—will continue at the same pace in 2026. For the average S&P 500 company, solid cash flow growth will drive solid cash spending growth. In our macro models, earnings growth is generally the most important driver of growth in each use of cash. According to consensus estimates, the median S&P 500 company should grow earnings by a solid 10% in 2026 and 11% in 2027. Consensus expects aggregate S&P 500 EPS will grow even faster (+22% in 2026 and +15% in 2027). However, these estimates are boosted by the largest stocks and some idiosyncratic factors that may not necessarily translate into uniform cash spending growth. The aggregate S&P 500 cash spending figures will be impacted by the spending priorities of the AI hyperscalers. The large public AI hyperscalers (AMZN, GOOGL, META, MSFT, ORCL) accounted for 34% of S&P 500 capex and R&D compared with 10% of S&P 500 buybacks and dividends in 2025. Consensus expects the hyperscalers to spend $755 billion on capex in 2026, representing growth of 83%. The outlook for capex growth in 2027 remains uncertain, but we expect a deceleration in the pace of growth. Increased hyperscaler capex has come at the expense of buybacks, which fell by 64% year/year for the group during 1Q. As our medium-term USD/JPY target (164) had already assumed that intervention is likely before the pair reached 162, events over the past week do not change our strategic outlook for Yen weakness. As a baseline, for a currency like the JPY—freely traded under a floating exchange rate regime and with a large, deep market—intervention cannot halt or reverse a trend determined by fundamentals. In the wake of the first intervention since July 2024, we received a number of questions from clients, which we fold into a handy Q&A below: Q1: Do you expect additional intervention in coming days, or does USD/JPY around 156 represent mission accom- plished? It is clear from recent developments that Japan’s currency authorities view USD/JPY 160 as a line in the sand. Whether additional intervention occurs will depend on how the market evolves, but estimated intervention to date totals around JPY 9 trillion—below the JPY 15 trillion seen in 2024—suggest- ing there is still room to intervene. As such, if USD/JPY rises to around 159–160 again, the likelihood of additional intervention is high. Commonly cited constraints on intervention—such as the idea that Japan cannot sell US Treasuries to finance interven- tion and therefore the JPY 25 trillion of “deposits” is effec- tively the intervention limit, or that the IMF AREAER free- floating criteria impose limits on the number of interventions —are not, in practice, hard constraints. records.text: European Rates Weekly 07 May 2026 Citi Research 8 The calls to defer NGEU repayments have resurfaced as increasing defence spending needs, combined with already elevated fiscal deficits, are adding pressure on EU government budgets. However, a deferral of NGEU repayments requires unanimous approval by the EU member states. This, whilst the EC has just launched the SAFE programme and is proposing more joint debt in its next budget, is unlikely to be acceptable to the fiscally conservative member states. A new EU programme for defence spending remains a possibility, but not in conjunction with deferral of NGEU repayments. The EC’s proposal, that shifts more of the NGEU repayment burden to future, might eventually be acceptable to the EU member states. Calls to delay NGEU repayments re-emerge. Whilst market focus was firmly on EU’s funding announcement last week, Bloomberg reported (28 April) that the European Commission is preparing an analysis of the possibility of delaying NGEU repayments. This topic is not new – The referral of NGEU repayments was already suggested by the former ECB President Draghi in his September 2024 report “The future of European competitiveness.” However, given that the end date of NGEU is fast approaching, these calls are likely to grow louder. Increasing defence spending needs will add further pressure on EU countries’ budgets. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 08 May 2026 Citi Research 5 Market Valuation: AI Risk Emerges as a Return Differentiator in B1 and B2 Software Loans The 75 software loans in our Tracker span the full range of speculative-grade credit ratings, with the vast majority concentrated in the B rating tier. The largest cohort sits at B2 comprising 32 loans — nearly 43% of the entire portfolio — followed by B3 with 18 loans (24%) and B1 with 13 loans (17%). Previously, we highlighted that the performance of software loans since February’s Claude Cowork release was mostly explained by their January-end price level. Our proprietary AI Risk Score (more details in the previous publication) also had considerable explanatory power for performance. We noted how monthly performance has been in line with the AI Risk Score. Score 3 outperformance in April stands out, but it wasn’t a broad-based recovery. Instead, a small number of idiosyncratic bounces drove up the average while the majority was still in decline. As a reminder, AI Risk Score range is 1 (low risk), 2 (medium risk), and 3 (high risk), comprising roughly 16%, 62%, and 22% by count, factoring in subsector risk, proprietary data, maturity, and credit quality. records.text: How investors have been rewarding changing corporate spending priorities The S&P 500 continues to notch new highs alongside rising earnings estimates. Results from the Q1 2026 earnings season have remained strong (Exhibit 26). S&P 500 year/year EPS growth for Q1 is now tracking at +17%, excluding the boost from mega-cap stakes in private companies. This represents the sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit earnings growth for the index. Since the start of 2026, the S&P 500 has risen by +8%, consensus forward 12-month EPS estimates have risen by +13%, and the P/E multiple has declined from 22x to 21x. However, the narrow recent breadth of both earnings revisions and the equity market rally creates the conditions for elevated Momentum factor volatility, as evidenced again this week. In addition to continued earnings strength, the Q1 earnings season has demonstrated a continued shift in corporate cash spending priorities. Among companies that have reported results, capex grew by +38% year/year during Q1 2026 while buybacks grew by just +1%. Like capex growth, R&D growth continued to accelerate, while dividend growth has remained relatively steady. NGEU repayments will start automatically in 2028. T o recap, the repayment of NGEU borrowing will start in 2028 (as communicated by the EC) and must be completed by 2058 as set in Article 5 (2) of the 2020 Own Resources Decision. Importantly, loans are repaid by the borrowing EU member states whilst grants are repaid from the EU budget. Article 5 (2) also restricts the annual principal repayments on NGEU grants to 7.5% of the total envelope for non-repayable support of c. €443bn (€360bn for RRF and €83bn for other NGEU programmes receiving NGEU funding, such as REACT-EU) which equates to c. €33bn/year. The EC’s 2028-34 budget proposal already proposes pushing more of the NGEU grant repayments into the future. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 9 Labor market indicators: back to the 40s We ran our indicator model of the private NFP employment subcategories, which assesses the probability of net job losses in the near future, reflected in the share of leading sectors weakening to a certain degree. The leading indicator in April ticked up to 44% from a (surprisingly) unrevised March reading of 37.5%, itself the lowest read since November '22. The move is similar to the private diffusion index which hit a recent peak at a solid 56.8 in March and fell back in April but remained above 50 at 53.8. The 'other' indicator remained flat at 46% relative to an also unrevised March, and the recent contour suggests a continued saw-tooth pattern around the 50% mark roughly since last summer. Overall, the picture suggests less stress in the labor market than six months ago, but historically, the pressure remains elevated in the broader 'other' category. This dynamic limits job opportunities for younger, lower-income workers who tend switch jobs more often, including college educated ones who are looking for jobs, even as aggregate employment remains relatively stable and workers aren’t getting fired. In addition, AI-related efficiency gains in some sectors like professional & business services likely reduced demand for junior roles or have made businesses cautious of hiring at the entry level until there is more clarity on AI efficiency, further constraining employment prospects at the lower end of the wage distribution. The unemployment rate for 20-24-year-olds peaked to decade-high levels of 9.2% in 2H25 (Exhibit 21). But the good news is that since then, it looks like the unemployment rate is past its peak, suggesting the worst of the pressure on this group linked to AI uptake & weak hiring has likely passed. Peruvian assets have built up some resistance to political volatility, but we see room for sizeable adjustments if the left-wing wins the presidential election. Over the last decade, political noise has become the rule in Peru, with eight presidents having taken office since 2016, reflecting a pro- found political instability. In that period, the response of Peruvian assets to major topics such as presidential removals from office has become quite limited, as investors got used to a state of political gridlock. We do not think this will remain the case if Roberto Sanchez ends up winning the presidential election, and see room for a strong adjustment in PEN. Election risks look asymmetric for PEN. Although we have already seen some correction in the currency, there is no evi- dence that PEN is carrying a sizeable risk premium, as it still remains close to our short-term fair value model estimate of 3.42. The lack of risk premia leaves plenty of room to catch up to a non-market friendly scenario, particularly if we take as reference the previous episode where far-left Pedro Castil- lo was elected beating Keiko Fujimori by a very thin margin (of 50.1% to 49.9%). International plc Bruna Skarica Chief UK Economist Bruna.Skarica@morganstanley.com +44 20 7425-9110 Local elections are taking place across England today, with Wales and Scotland voting in their national elections too. In this note we summarise the latest polling, our latest thoughts on fiscal policy and the next steps in the government's legislative agenda. What is happening? Local government elections take place at least every four years. Not all local government elections take place at the same time. Local authorities can elect all the councilors every four years, half the councilors every two years, and a third of the councilors every year for three years. Today's local elections are the biggest set of elections in this parliament, covering 5k council seats across 136 councils in England. Wales and Scotland are also electing their representatives in the devolved national parliaments. What are polls saying | England: Local elections are being held across all 32 London boroughs, as well as in councils across the North East, North West, Yorkshire, Midlands and the South. Around half of the councils only have elections for a third or half of their seats, which means that a party could theoretically win a large number seats, without gaining control over a proportional number of councils. records.text: US Economics Weekly8 May 2026 ab 4 Back in the early 2000s, macro labor was beginning two important debates. One was over labor force participation rates and not only whether the long trend increases had leveled off, but whether a long run decline was getting underway. Another was over whether labor’s share was stable. Long assumed by macroeconomists to be stable, at the same time some of us were arguing demographic shifts would push the participation rate lower in the coming decades, we were also arguing that labor’s share was not stable, and would likely head lower too. An earlier debate also resurfaced recently. David Card shared the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. One of his most famous papers, jointly authored with the late Alan Krueger, showed that employment did not fall after an increase in the minimum wage in New Jersey. (2) . Many readers thought that paper argued the increases in minimum wages had no effect on employment. However, if one asked David, he would say the main point of the research implied that (due to monopsonistic labor markets) in some labor markets, firms have sufficient bargaining power to set market wages far enough below costs that an increase in wages would not affect employment. Today’s wage bargaining is primarily in a service sector economy. Contracts are typically bilateral, and often at will. Now, this is not an argument for restricting the labor market either. The pickup in productivity growth has become more persistent and is likely at least partly driven by the impact of AI related investment. In our note, "Economic Impact of AI", we estimated what we thought would be the lift structurally and not for reasons like catch-up, or sectoral shifts, which are also playing a role in the strengthening of productivity growth seen in the latest data. Since the onset of the pandemic, nonfarm business sector productivity has risen 2.2% at an annual rate, a solid pickup from the 1.6% pace from 2004 to 2019. Chart below. As a small share of overall nonresidential structures investment, data center spending isn't offsetting the weakness elsewhere. State and local construction was flat in February (-0.0%) and fell 0.1% in March after a 0.4% increase in January. records.text: Metal Matters 08 May 2026 Citi Research 5 Copper supply also exposed to Strait of Hormuz closure via higher energy pricing and potential sulphur shortages In the event of a prolonged Strait of Hormuz closure, we see supply‑side adjustments acting as another meaningful offset to any cyclical demand shock from higher energy prices, with scrap most exposed. We think the dominant transmission channel on the supply side is scrap, where elevated fuel and logistics costs can inflate the scrap recovery cost curve, with risks of sulfur shortage on mine supply likely to constrain output to a far lesser extent. In Figure 1, we show indicatively that while a copper demand shock can drive prices towards marginal cost, sufficient producer cost inflation can see copper prices rise higher (even as producer margins are compressed). Marginal copper scrap supply is more cost sensitive to energy price shocks than mine supply and is most at risk of constraint from higher energy pricing. Scrap recovery is both energy‑ and transport‑intensive, leaving collection, processing, and remelting costs highly exposed to power, fuel, and logistics inflation. This sensitivity is particularly important given that scrap drives the majority of modelled copper supply growth this year, against flat mine output expectations. records.text: US Daily Data Recap7 May 2026 ab 3 Job cut announcements at 74K in April Job cut announcements rose 34K to 74K on a seasonally-adjusted basis in April, according to the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. On a not-seasonally- adjusted basis, job cuts rose 23K to 83K. On a four-month moving average basis, at ~56K seasonally-adjusted layoff announcements sit modestly above the pre-pandemic range (see chart below). In the press release (link here), Andy Challenger noted, " Technology companies continue to announce large-scale cuts and are leading all industries in layoff announcements. They are also often citing AI spend and innovation. Regardless of whether individual jobs are being replaced by AI, the money for those roles is." Job cut announcements in the technology sector rose 22K to 24K in April, seasonally adjusted. On a NSA basis, the technology sector announced 33K job cuts in April, for a total of 85K cuts in 2026 year-to-date. That is above the 64K cuts in this sector announced for the same period last year, and the highest year-to-date total since the 114K in March 2023. Government entities announced plans to cut 9K jobs, the highest monthly total since the sector cut 217K jobs in March 2025, alongside DOGE actions. Second round price pressures from energy price hikes will not fully be reflected on services and other sectors yet, and pose upside risks to the inflation outlook. We think larger than expected price increases for food (3.7% m/m) and clothing (8.9% m/m) already point to early evidence of second - round pressures and are not just the result of seasonal factors. In this vein, we find that the monthly seasonally adjusted (trend indicator) in core indicators (2.46%) remains uncomfortably high. Domestic demand resilience into the shock: Services inflation was 3.03% m/m, mainly due transportation services (6.2% m/m), though restaurant prices also jumped by 3.5% m/m, reflecting persistent services inertia. Türkiye’s economy remained resilient into the latest supply shock, and we think the quick resumption of service price momentum indicates slower-than-expected cooling of domestic demand. Year-end CPI 2.5pp higher: Net net, the April CPI details reveal a higher inflation path than we had forecast. We raise our December CPI inflation forecast from 27.0% y/y to 29.5%. We see upside risks to these numbers , mainly dependent on the duration of the Middle East conflict and how quickly energy prices can realistically retrace (our base case is for Brent at USD85/bbl by Q4). Across the quality spectrum, property price increases for top-tier properties have lagged the overall market, likely reflecting the excess supply dynamic. We expect this to reverse this year, as top-tier supply should be limited and renters' preference for newly constructed top-end properties is likely to remain in place amid low home affordability. records.text: a rate hike (h>0), the wage threat is activated, the rule-based rate increases by 𝜃𝛽𝑤 and the policy rate rises by h. The resulting policy gap is: g(h, w) = g + 𝜃𝛽𝑤 − ℎ This expression serves to see that a modest rate hike can leave the policy gap wider than the prevailing policy gap if: g + 𝜃𝛽𝑤 − ℎ > 𝑔 ℎ < 𝜃𝛽𝑤 Thus, any positive hike below 𝜃𝛽𝑤 triggers the minimum-wage shock but does not offset the additional increase in the policy rate prescribed by the rule. In this case, the final policy gap is larger than under a ‘no hike’ scenario. In Figure 2, we demonstrate the policy gap under three scenarios for the minimum wage (5%, 10% and 15%). Figure 3 shows the parameter values used for the exercise. This simple analysis, ​which still excludes credibility costs (see page 3)​, ​suggests that a rate hike of less than 200bp could have left BanRep with a policy gap larger than the one it faced before the monetary policy meeting if the minimum-wage increase was at least 10%. The exercise has limitations as BanRep faced, ex-ante, uncertainty about the magnitude of any forthcoming minimum-wage rise and the costs associated with a more strained relationship with the government. records.text: 6 Retail trading identification, an introduction: Since decimal pricing (2001) and Reg-NMS (2005), size-based filters no longer capture retail activity (Hvidkjær 2008). New strategies have emerged, most notably the BJZZ rule-based algorithm. Academic literature review – BJZZ and successors. Boehmer et al. (2021) define BJZZ: all marketable retail orders are treated as off-exchange and are identified by sub-penny ‘buckets’. Empirical validation of BJZZ: Barber et al. (2024) submitted ~5k retail orders and found BJZZ flagged only 35% or so of their own trades. Using the Lee-Ready rule with NBBO raised signing accuracy from 72% to 95%. Execution-quality literature. Ernst et al. (2023) used BJZZ-identified flow to study wholesalers’ price-improvement incentives, emphasizing the role of ‘odd-lot’ orders. Many recent execution-quality studies treat BJZZ-identified trades as a representative retail sample despite its imperfect signing record Trade-signing methodology. Battalio et al. (2026) improve look-ahead bias by employing a lagged, latency-free NBBO, achieving about 99% signing accuracy. This is BNP Paribas’ current approach, leveraging direct exchange feeds for NBBO extraction. Key takeaways from the literature review: Retail identification moved from size-based to price-bucket-based after market-structure reforms, with BJZZ being the most widely adopted rule-based solution. While the exact impact of this energy price shock on core inflation is hard to predict, we can try to come up with a range of estimates. For our low inflation scenario, we assume that current oil futures pricing is realized, and oil prices fall back to below $80/bbl by December. In that scenario, any possible impacts from higher energy prices will mostly be reversed by the end of the year. Shelter inflation will continue close to 0.2% MoM and core goods inflation will continue at its current 3m average of ~0.08% MoM. For core services ex-shelter inflation, we assume it will continue to follow the pattern from last year just as it did in January and February. In this scenario, we assume any impact from oil prices to airfares will reverse in the second half of this year. This leads to core inflation of around 2.5% by the end of this year. We think it is very possible that the eventual reality will end up being closer to this scenario. For our second scenario, we assume that oil prices will stay at these elevated levels for the rest of this year. Shelter inflation will be slightly higher at 0.25% MoM. Core goods will see some impact from higher oil prices, and so we assume 0.15% MoM core goods inflation. That is more than the core goods inflation that we saw in 2025 with all the tariff impacts. This likely reflects continued strong aluminium smelter margins, incentivising maximum throughput, as well as lower demand from solar and EVs/ appliances this year. China mainly exports aluminium in the form of semi-fabricated products (400-500 ktpm) rather than unwrought metal (~45 ktpm). Most upgrades focused on improving operating performance, with some also citing firms improving their capital structure through paying down debt via proceeds from IPOs or increasing reliance on unsecured debt. Rating downgrades’ rationale spanned softening demand, secular challenges, cost inflation, elevated debt and weak liquidity. We do not want to overstate the importance of these improving credit trends because rating changes can often be reactive and somewhat backward looking. In short, the trend could reverse. Instead, we think it is remarkable that rating agency actions have differed to such a large extent from the collective perception of quality. A market observer looking only at media headlines would conclude corporate credit quality is nosediving. records.text: Japan has a track record of improving its energy efficiency during periods of n rising crude oil prices. In particular since 2000, a period in which crude oil prices have remained elevated, its energy efficiency has improved continuously. The driver of the improvement is the manufacturing sector, especially processing industries. Since 2000, the improvements in energy efficiency—particularly in the n processing industries—have led to an increase in the capital-labor ratio through the accumulation of energy-efficient capital stock and a rise in total factor productivity (TFP) through improvements in production and operational processes, supporting labor productivity growth. For Japan, an energy-importing country, higher energy prices signal n deterioration in terms of trade, which drags down economic growth via a decrease in national income. However, improvements in energy efficiency serve to boost economic growth on a slightly longer term horizon via productivity gains. With corporates in Japan currently viewing decarbonization as a key driver of n capex, improvements in energy efficiency are likely to continue. Refining is essentially the process of separating a barrel of crude into different products according to boiling points. Gasoline, jet fuel and diesel represent the three dominant fuels produced from a barrel of oil. While modern refiners have some flexibility to shift output based on prices or seasonal demand, they are ultimately constrained by both chemistry and hardware. A refinery cannot simply decide one morning to turn an entire barrel of crude into jet fuel just because jet prices spiked overnight. Crude oil itself is not a single homogenous substance. Every barrel contains a different mix of molecules, and those differences largely determine what product a refinery can produce from it. Light crude flows more freely and contains a higher share of smaller hydrocarbon molecules, naturally yielding more gasoline and naphtha. Heavy crude is thick and dense, like molasses, and is packed with large, more complex molecules, tending to yield more diesel, fuel oil and residual products. At its core, refining is a mass-balance system: you cannot get out more than you put in. Refining is therefore fundamentally a zero-sum game. At the same time, fiscal pressures are high, no matter who the Labour leader is, in our view. All in all, this may end up being more of a distributional issue than one of fiscal laxity. Germany: budget gyrations and industry surprises Germany’s signal-to-noise ratio is deteriorating. The 2027 budget planning has started, naturally capturing attention after last year’s innovations. We go through the details in our main piece. Not surprisingly, bigger net funding needs have captured some attention but for us the main points are: 1) Fiscal stimulus (c1.5% of GDP) will peak in 2026E, reflected in our forecasts for a while now. The new 2027 budget only creates a relatively small top-up (0.2%). 2) Filling budget holes has moved the debate to restrictive policy before stimulus has had time to kick in. This was meant to happen eventually but those gaps have largely been ignored by markets. 3) Political tensions are high. We work under the assumption that a 2027 budget will be passed, including the required corrective measures. But our conviction is low and potential is building for an idiosyncratic policy uncertainty shock. Meanwhile, hard data has delivered some better surprises lately. records.text: Metal Matters 08 May 2026 Citi Research 4 Military-related copper demand likely resilient with upside to counter growth risks from geopolitical deterioration There are clear growth and cyclical copper demand risks associated with escalating conflict and geopolitical friction, such as current regional tension in the Middle East. However, such escalation also poses counterfactual upside for global military spend and related copper consumption, which can help cushion any broader cyclical demand impact. Consensus estimates point to resilient military spending, supporting related copper consumption, with upside in response to any geopolitical escalation. Consensus estimates imply modest growth in global military spend in the coming years. If we assume a linear relationship with copper consumption, this points to resilient military-related copper consumption at higher levels and modest growth in the coming years, However, scenarios of escalating military tension in the Middle East or elsewhere could see military demand for copper (which we roughly estimate at ~2.5 Mtpa, or ~9% of global consumption) soar higher as observed in recent years following the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war. This slowdown reduces the cycle's ability to buffer a shock, increasing the risk of stagnation or even recession. Governments have responded to the current energy shock with fiscal measures, but these are significantly less extensive than those deployed in 2022. The 2026 inflation shock is smaller and the starting position for public finances is weaker. But part of the reason for the smaller fiscal response is also the fact that the Commission has not triggered either of the escape clauses from the EU fiscal rules. In this blog we look at the difference between the General Escape Clause (GEC) and National Escape Clause (NEC). Roughly speaking, the triggers are a severe economic downturn for the former and circumstances outside the control of a member state for the latter. In the absence of severe recession, countries under Excessive Deficit Procedures are likely to push for the latter. records.text: The predominance of 5-year fixed mortgages in Canada creates the risk of mortgage payment shocks Most of the mortgages in Canada have a 5-year fixed period, after which the mortgage must be renewed or refinanced. A recent report from the Bank of Canada notes that 60% of mortgages in Canada are expected to renew in 2025 or 2026. The rise in mortgage rates resulting from the Central Bank’s substantial rate hikes in 2022 has led to payment shocks for borrowers whose five-year terms are set to expire in 2025 or 2026 (Exhibit 6 and 7). On the other hand, US homeowners benefit from a 30-year fixed rate mortgage, which keeps payments stable for the life of the mortgage. Most US borrowers currently enjoy rates that are well below prevailing rates (Exhibit 8). A close analogy to the payment shocks experienced by Canadian homeowners currently are the payment shocks experienced by borrowers who had teaser-rate products pre-GFC in the US. When their rates reset to prevailing market rates, it resulted in substantial payment increases and significant weakness in the housing market. The US market is well insulated from such shocks currently vs. the Canadian market. To be clear, while the payment shocks in Canada can weaken the housing market, we are not forecasting any GFC-style downturn. In addition, seasonal patterns paired with a slightly less punishing seasonal factor this year relative to prior years suggest a moderate increase in continuing claims in the first week of May. One potential contributor to the recent low level of continuing claims is an increase in exhaustions (when benefits run out after 26 weeks of benefits in any 52-week period). In March, the latest data, exhaustions bounced back after declines in January and February. 26 weeks ago, in October 2025, claims were sawtoothing from week to week, but the 4-week moving average of initial claims generally trended down from October through the rest of the fall, so in the coming weeks, there will likely be fewer claimants exhausting their benefits, possibly exerting less downward pressure on continuing claims. Aggressive hiking cycle is priced in: The KRW rates market has been pricing in lot of rate hikes since the start of this year, but we think elevated inflation expectations linked to the Middle East conflict have pushed pricing into overly aggressive territory. Market levels currently imply about more than four hikes (or 120bp) from the Bank of Korea over the next 12 months, a scenario we do think is supported by fundamentals. In our base case, the BoK could hike by 50bp over the next year if oil prices remain high and growth continues to perform well (see South Korea: Implications of higher growth and inflation, dated 27 April). However, the BoK is likely to adopt a data-dependent approach rather than being pre-emptive – and is unlikely to rush into rapid rate hikes without clear signs of second-round inflationary effects (e.g. sustained wage-price spirals). records.text: US Rates Weekly 08 May 2026 Citi Research 9 Short end: Excessively managing the TGA? Repo markets this week continued to show signs that liquidity in the system is plentiful. Yesterday SOFR fixed 5bp below IORB, the lowest level since early April and Aug-25 before then (Figure 14). Notably we also saw effective FF tick 1 bp lower yesterday. We think this move could be a one-off event, driven by a combination of higher FF volume and a relatively lower TGCR rate. On the volume side, we had argued before that FF volumes were likely to pick up following the April 15 Tax Day, and as we show Figure 15, FF volume is back to the levels from last summer. It is possible the deluge of liquidity via the Fed’s Reserve Management Purchases has limited demand for FHLB advances, and thus there is an overallocation to Fed funds by the FHLBs. That, combined with TGCR below EFFR, likely put downward pressure on EFFR. For now, we do not expect to see EFFR continuing to move lower and instead think it is possible this move lower is undone in the near term. We think May SOFR/FF is somewhat insulated from this move in EFFR. Or in other words, EFFR will only keep going lower in the short term if TGCR stays roughly under 3.6%; thus SOFR/FF probably realizes at higher levels if EFFR keeps falling. Tech underperformed non-fins by a net 16bp across that three-year stretch. Research 2 Situation and outlook for municipal finances Summary The key points below and the following charts are based on our German -language study 'Im Schatten der Fiskalexpansion: Deutschlands Gemeinden in großen Finanznöten' (In the Shadow of Fiscal Expansion: Germany's municipalities facing large financial difficulties), which was published on May 8, 2026. — The municipalities are in a major budget crisis, which escalated in 2025. With an aggregated financial deficit of almost EUR 32 bn, the core and extra budgets at the municipal level recorded the highest deficit since German reunification. — The financial problem is a nationwide phenomenon that has affected municipalities in almost all federal states. At 0.7% of GDP or 7.5% of expenditure, the aggregated 2025 financial deficit even surpasses previous values from the time of the global financial and economic crisis (2009/10) and the early 2000s. — The municipalities’ budget problems are not mainly cyclical; they are primarily rooted in the federal financial system. While municipalities bear around 25% of total public expenditure (excluding spending by social security funds), they receive only about 14% of total tax revenues.
